title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A sphere gives the simplest example
text:
A sphere gives the simplest example
Constrain a nonzero vector to the sphere \(\lVert w\rVert_2=R\). Differentiating \(\lVert w+tZ\rVert_2^2=R^2\) at \(t=0\) gives the tangent condition
\[
\langle w,Z\rangle=0.
\]
Let \(g\) be the ambient loss gradient. Its tangent projection is
\[
g_T=g-\frac{\langle w,g\rangle}{R^2}w.
\]
Under a Euclidean displacement budget \(\lVert Z\rVert_2\leq\epsilon\), the constrained linear problem has solution
\[
Z_*=-\epsilon\frac{g_T}{\lVert g_T\rVert_2}
\]
when \(g_T\ne0\). Choose zero if \(g_T=0\). This follows because a tangent displacement pairs with \(g\) exactly as it pairs with \(g_T\), and Cauchy-Schwarz solves the remaining support problem.
The ambient gradient need not be tangent. We did not assume scale invariance of the loss here. The tangent condition comes from the weight constraint itself.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A tangent step is still only locally on the sphere
text:
A tangent step is still only locally on the sphere
For tangent \(Z\),
\[
\lVert w+Z\rVert_2^2=R^2+\lVert Z\rVert_2^2.
\]
The trial point leaves the sphere by a second-order amount. A radial retraction brings it back:
\[
\mathcal R_w(Z)=R\frac{w+Z}{\lVert w+Z\rVert_2}.
\]
Its derivative at zero returns \(Z\), so it agrees with the tangent displacement to first order. It is not an assertion that a finite straight step lies on a curved surface.
For \(w=(1,0)\) and \(Z=(0,1/2)\), the trial point is \((1,1/2)\) and the retracted point is \((2,1)/\sqrt5\). The rotation is \(\arctan(1/2)\approx26.57^\circ\). More generally,
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{\lVert Z\rVert_2}{R},
\qquad
\lVert\mathcal R_w(Z)-w\rVert_2=2R\sin(\theta/2).
\]
Tangent length, arc length \(R\theta\), and chord length are close for small steps. They are different finite-step quantities.



A tangent displacement leaves the unit circle at a trial point. Radial retraction returns it to the circle while preserving its new direction. The tangent length, rotation angle, and chord length are distinct.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: The Stiefel constraint preserves more than one length
text:
The Stiefel constraint preserves more than one length
For \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\geq n\), the column Stiefel constraint is
\[
W^\top W=I_n.
\]
It fixes each column length and every pairwise column inner product. Differentiating gives
\[
W^\top Z+Z^\top W=0.
\]
Under Frobenius geometry, the tangent projection of an ambient matrix \(G\) is
\[
\Pi_W(G)=G-W\operatorname{sym}(W^\top G),
\qquad \operatorname{sym}(A)=\frac{A+A^\top}{2}.
\]
The removed term is Frobenius-orthogonal to every tangent matrix. A fixed Frobenius-radius support step therefore normalizes \(\Pi_W(G)\), just as in the sphere example.
A convenient retraction is
\[
\mathcal R_W(Z)=(W+Z)
\left[(W+Z)^\top(W+Z)\right]^{-1/2}.
\]
For tangent \(Z\), the Gram matrix in brackets is \(I+Z^\top Z\), which is positive definite. The retracted matrix has orthonormal columns and equals \(W+Z\) to first order.
The row-orthonormal version applies when the matrix shape calls for it. A rectangular matrix cannot generally have both orthonormal rows and orthonormal columns. The orientation of the constraint is part of the specification.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A different tangent norm changes the support problem
text:
A different tangent norm changes the support problem
Replacing the Frobenius budget by a spectral budget gives
\[
\min_Z\langle G,Z\rangle_F
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
W^\top Z+Z^\top W=0,
\quad\lVert Z\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\epsilon.
\]
This is not the unconstrained polar problem from Part 6. Projecting an ambient polar factor is not automatically its solution.
For a small counterexample, set \(W=I_2\) and
\[
G=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The tangent matrices are skew-symmetric. The ambient polar factor is
\[
P=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its Frobenius tangent projection is \(J/\sqrt{10}\), where \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). This has operator norm \(1/\sqrt{10}\) and support value \(1/\sqrt{10}\). The feasible tangent matrix \(J\) has operator norm one and support value one.
For descent, negate these directions. Projection after dualization wasted available budget in this example. Renormalizing repairs this particular two-dimensional case, but that is not a general derivation of a constrained spectral oracle.
This is why manifold methods must solve the support problem for their actual tangent set and norm. The operations do not come with permission to commute.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A sphere, an oblique set, and Stiefel are different constraints
text:
A sphere, an oblique set, and Stiefel are different constraints
A Frobenius sphere fixes one total matrix length while allowing its singular values and column lengths to redistribute. An oblique constraint fixes each column length, while leaving the angles between columns free. Stiefel additionally fixes those angles to be right angles.
For example,
\[
W=\begin{pmatrix}1&\cos\phi\\0&\sin\phi\end{pmatrix}
\]
has unit columns for every \(\phi\). At \(\phi=60^\circ\), its singular values are \(\sqrt{3/2}\) and \(\sqrt{1/2}\), so its condition number is \(\sqrt3\). As \(\phi\) approaches zero, it becomes nearly rank deficient despite retaining both column lengths.
A weight constraint can therefore remove useful functional freedoms, not merely redundant coordinate scales. Whether it preserves an architecture’s function class needs a separate argument. The later shared-gain examples will make that issue concrete.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: What the optimizer must specify
text:
What the optimizer must specify
A complete constrained update needs a weight set, its tangent directions, a norm or metric on those directions, and a finite-step return map. It also needs an account of optimizer memory when the base update has a momentum state.
Fixing only the weight radius leaves the update geometry unspecified. Fixing only the update norm leaves the weight trajectory free to drift. The choices can cooperate, but they answer different questions.
Next we examine a wrapper that explicitly controls both weight and proposal norms, and ask what that control does and does not say about angular schedules.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: Try staying on the constraint set
text:
Try staying on the constraint set

On a radius-two sphere, take a tangent displacement of length one. What is the rotation after radial retraction?
Verify that \(W^\top\Pi_W(G)+\Pi_W(G)^\top W=0\) whenever \(W^\top W=I\).
Why does the projected polar factor in the \(2\times2\) example fail to maximize spectral-unit support?



Answer sketches


\(\theta=\arctan(1/2)\approx26.57^\circ\). The tangent length is one, not the angle in radians.
Substitute the projection formula. The remaining expression is \(W^\top G+G^\top W-2\operatorname{sym}(W^\top G)=0\).
It equals \(J/\sqrt{10}\), while \(J\) itself remains feasible and gives a larger pairing with \(G\).

Yo twin, go read…
Jeremy Bernstein, Modular Manifolds (2025), especially the sphere example and Manifold Muon discussion, separates weight constraints, tangent norms, support directions, and retractions. Its spectral manifold problem should not be replaced silently by a Frobenius projection.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The gradient first acts as a measuring device
text:
The gradient first acts as a measuring device
Let \(L(W)\) be differentiable, with matrix gradient \(G=\nabla L(W)\). Its first-order change along a perturbation is
\[
\mathrm dL_W[\Delta W]
=\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F
=\operatorname{tr}(G^\top\Delta W).
\]
At this point, \(G\) represents a linear functional: give it a proposed update and it reports a scalar slope. The Frobenius pairing is how we write that derivative in matrix coordinates. It does not require us to measure the size of an update with the Frobenius norm.
Let \(N\) be our chosen norm on perturbations. For a radius \(\epsilon>0\), choose the update that minimizes the linear model:
\[
\min_{N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon}\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F.
\]
The constraint is the missing definition of steepest. Without it, a negative linear slope can be made arbitrarily negative just by scaling up the step.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The dual norm is the support value
text:
The dual norm is the support value
Define the dual norm by
\[
N^*(G)=\max_{N(D)\leq1}\langle G,D\rangle_F.
\]
Because a norm ball is symmetric, minimizing over a radius-\(\epsilon\) ball gives
\[
\min_{N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon}\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F
=-\epsilon N^*(G).
\]
If \(D_*(G)\) is a maximizing unit-ball direction, one optimal update is
\[
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon D_*(G).
\]
The dual norm gives the best linear decrease per unit budget. The maximizing direction tells us how to attain it. Those are different outputs of the same support problem.
This is standard normed steepest descent. Boyd and Vandenberghe’s Section 9.4 develops the geometric interpretation, and Bernstein and Newhouse’s Sections 3.1 and 3.2 use it to construct layerwise duality maps.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Frobenius geometry recovers the normalized gradient
text:
Frobenius geometry recovers the normalized gradient
For \(N(D)=\lVert D\rVert_F\), Cauchy-Schwarz gives
\[
\langle G,D\rangle_F
\leq\lVert G\rVert_F\lVert D\rVert_F.
\]
For nonzero \(G\), equality is attained by \(D_*=G/\lVert G\rVert_F\). Thus the Frobenius norm is self-dual, and the fixed-radius step is
\[
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon\frac{G}{\lVert G\rVert_F}.
\]
That is a normalized gradient update. Ordinary gradient descent, \(-\eta G\), also uses this direction, but its radius is \(\eta\lVert G\rVert_F\) rather than a fixed \(\epsilon\).
Now change the norm while keeping \(G\) fixed.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: A spectral budget produces a polar direction
text:
A spectral budget produces a polar direction
Let \(N(D)=\lVert D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\), the largest singular value. Write a compact singular value decomposition using only the positive singular values of \(G\):
\[
G=U\Sigma V^\top
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_i v_i^\top.
\]
For any \(D\) with operator norm at most one,
\[
\langle G,D\rangle_F
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_i^\top Dv_i
\leq\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i.
\]
The bound follows because \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) are unit vectors and \(\lvert u_i^\top Dv_i\rvert\leq1\). It is attained by the partial polar factor
\[
D_*(G)=UV^\top.
\]
This matrix has singular value one on each active singular mode. Consequently,
\[
N^*(G)=\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}}
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i,
\qquad
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon UV^\top.
\]
The spectral norm’s dual is the nuclear norm, not the spectral norm again. I use the subscript \(\mathrm{op}\) for the largest singular value and \(\mathrm{nuc}\) for their sum. The asterisk on \(N^*\) means duality.
If \(G\) is rank deficient, the compact polar factor is one maximizer. Additional components on unused subspaces can also be optimal if they stay feasible. If \(G=0\), choose the zero update. These cases should not be implemented by dividing blindly by a zero norm or singular value.
This operation changes the singular values of the update direction. It does not impose a norm constraint on the current weight matrix \(W\).

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The same derivative, three different unit balls
text:
The same derivative, three different unit balls
Take \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\) and a budget radius \(\epsilon=0.1\).
Under a Frobenius budget,
\[
\Delta W_F=-\frac{0.1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{diag}(3,1),
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_F\rangle_F=-0.1\sqrt{10}\approx-0.316228.
\]
Under a spectral budget,
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{op}}=-0.1 I,
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_{\mathrm{op}}\rangle_F=-0.4.
\]
For comparison, a nuclear-norm budget has dual value \(\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=3\). One optimal update spends the whole budget on the leading singular mode:
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{nuc}}=-0.1\operatorname{diag}(1,0),
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_{\mathrm{nuc}}\rangle_F=-0.3.
\]



Diagonal slices of the Frobenius, spectral, and nuclear unit balls. For the same derivative with diagonal entries three and one, their maximizing directions lie on a circle, a square, and a diamond respectively.


The figure shows positive support directions \(D_*\). The actual descent update is \(-\epsilon D_*\). Restricting the picture to diagonal matrices is enough to display maximizers for this diagonal \(G\).
The larger decrease under the spectral budget is not an optimizer victory. It is a comparison of different feasible sets. The spectral step has Frobenius norm \(0.1\sqrt2\), so it would not fit inside the Frobenius budget of radius \(0.1\).
There is another useful comparison inside the spectral ball. Simply dividing the gradient by its spectral norm gives
\[
\frac{G}{\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/3).
\]
It is feasible, but its support value is \(10/3\), below the optimum four. Normalization alone does not solve a general support problem.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Carry the RMS ruler through the dual calculation
text:
Carry the RMS ruler through the dual calculation
Part 5 measured a dense-layer perturbation with
\[
N(D)=k\lVert D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},
\qquad k=\sqrt{n/m}.
\]
Its unit ball allows operator norm \(1/k\). Scaling the support problem therefore gives
\[
N^*(G)=\frac1k\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}},
\qquad
D_*(G)=\frac1k UV^\top
=\sqrt{m/n}\,UV^\top.
\]
The width factor reverses because a larger primal norm makes the feasible unit ball smaller. For a nine-input, four-output layer, the polar factor is multiplied by \(2/3\) to have unit RMS-to-RMS norm.
This is the dense-layer duality map in Bernstein and Newhouse’s Example 3. The activation ruler, its induced matrix norm, and its support direction are three connected parts of one construction.


What changes for an embedding lookup?

For Euclidean output measurements, Part 5’s lookup budget was \(N(D)=\max_j\lVert D[:,j]\rVert_2\). Each column can use its unit budget independently, so
\[
N^*(G)=\sum_j\lVert G[:,j]\rVert_2,
\qquad
D_*[:,j]=\frac{G[:,j]}{\lVert G[:,j]\rVert_2}
\]
for nonzero columns. Choose zero for a zero gradient column. With an RMS output ruler, multiply both the dual value and the direction by \(\sqrt m\).
The largest-column update norm is paired with a sum of gradient-column norms. It does not mean spending the entire update on only one column. This is the Embed duality map in the paper’s Example 4.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: A direction and a step-size model are separate choices
text:
A direction and a step-size model are separate choices
The fixed-radius support problem is not the only way to choose a step. Consider instead
\[
\min_\Delta\left\{\langle G,\Delta\rangle_F
+\frac1{2\eta}N(\Delta)^2\right\},\qquad \eta>0.
\]
At radius \(r\), the best linear term is \(-rN^*(G)\). Minimizing \(-rN^*(G)+r^2/(2\eta)\) gives \(r=\eta N^*(G)\), hence one minimizer is
\[
\Delta_*=-\eta N^*(G)D_*(G).
\]
For the Frobenius norm, this recovers \(-\eta G\). For the spectral norm, it gives \(-\eta\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}}UV^\top\). A fixed-radius polar update omits that dual-magnitude factor because it solves a different optimization problem.
Neither linear model automatically controls a large finite loss change. A useful quadratic upper bound, a line search, or an appropriately chosen small step needs its own justification. The norm describes which perturbations are allowed. Curvature describes what the loss does along them.
The same care applies to momentum. If we replace \(G\) by a buffer \(M\), dualization solves the support problem for the linear functional represented by \(M\). The actual current derivative is still \(G\). A norm-feasible buffer step need not be a descent direction for the current loss.
We now know how to choose a direction for one module’s geometry. The next post asks how those local budgets fit together across the network, and why Modula uses a weighted maximum to combine them.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Try solving the support problem
text:
Try solving the support problem

For \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\), compare the spectral-budget support values of \(G/\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\) and \(UV^\top\).
For \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,0)\), give a compact polar maximizer and a different spectral-unit-ball maximizer with the same support value.
Under a Euclidean lookup budget with gradient columns \((3,4)\) and \((0,2)\), find the dual value and one maximizing matrix.
Let \(L(W)=\lVert W\rVert_F^2/2\) at \(W=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\). A spectral-budget step is \(\Delta=-\epsilon I\). Compute the exact loss change at \(\epsilon=5\), and compare it with the linear prediction.



Answer sketches


They are \(10/3\) and four. Both proposals have spectral norm one, but only the polar factor attains the support maximum here.
The compact polar factor is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). The matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1)\) also has operator norm one and support value three. The unused second mode does not affect the linear objective.
The dual value is \(5+2=7\). Normalize each column separately, giving columns \((3/5,4/5)\) and \((0,1)\).
The exact change is \(-4\epsilon+\epsilon^2\), so it equals five. The linear prediction is \(-20\). A direction that is steepest for the linear model can still overshoot badly.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Section 9.4 and Appendix A.1.6, explains normed steepest descent, dual norms, and the spectral-nuclear pairing. Keep the normalized direction separate from its dual-norm-scaled version.

Section 5 discusses efficient matrix iterations. The exact SVD support calculation above does not by itself specify a complete practical optimizer, its momentum convention, or an approximation algorithm.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Choose a buffer convention we can actually analyze
text:
Choose a buffer convention we can actually analyze
Use the following momentum update with decoupled decay:
\[
m_t=\beta m_{t-1}+g_t,
\qquad g_t=\nabla L_t(w_t),
\]
\[
w_{t+1}=a_t w_t-\eta_t m_t,
\qquad a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t>0.
\]
Here \(0\leq\beta<1\), \(m_{-1}=0\), \(\eta_t>0\), and \(\lambda_t\geq0\). The buffer stores gradients before multiplication by the learning rate. There is no \((1-\beta)\) factor, dampening, Nesterov lookahead, or decay term inside this buffer.
That last choice matters. A coupled quadratic penalty would instead give
\[
m_t^{\mathrm{coupled}}
=\beta m_{t-1}^{\mathrm{coupled}}+g_t+\lambda_t w_t,
\qquad
w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t m_t^{\mathrm{coupled}}.
\]
The penalty then persists in the buffer. With zero initial buffers, the first weight update agrees with our decoupled version, but the stored states differ and later weight updates generally diverge. With \(\beta=0\) the distinction disappears for these equations.
Loshchilov and Hutter’s decoupled-weight-decay paper, Section 2 and Algorithm 1, is a useful reference for keeping these choices separate. Its buffer stores a learning-rate-scaled contribution. Our displayed convention stores the unscaled gradient, so a changing learning rate requires its own bookkeeping.
For the geometry below, assume the same blockwise forward invariance as before. Then \(g_t\perp w_t\). The statement is about the data gradient, not automatically about \(m_t\).

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Split the proposed update at the current weight
text:
Split the proposed update at the current weight
Write \(w_t=R_t e_t\) with unit \(e_t\). Decompose the buffer into
\[
p_t=\langle e_t,m_t\rangle,
\qquad v_t=m_t-p_t e_t,
\qquad v_t\perp e_t.
\]
The scalar \(p_t\) is the radial component of the buffer. The vector \(v_t\) is its tangent component. The weight update becomes
\[
w_{t+1}
=(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t)e_t-\eta_t v_t.
\]
Everything about this one step is now a right triangle. Its new radius is
\[
R_{t+1}^2
=(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t)^2+\eta_t^2\|v_t\|_2^2.
\]
If \(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t>0\), the rotation satisfies
\[
\tan\theta_t
=\frac{\eta_t\|v_t\|_2}{a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t}.
\]
The denominator contains information that \(\eta_t\|m_t\|_2/R_t\) loses. If the denominator is zero or negative, use
\[
\theta_t=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(\eta_t\|v_t\|_2,\ a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t\right),
\]
with an angle in \([0,\pi]\) and a nonzero resulting weight. A negative denominator can mean a rotation beyond \(90^\circ\). Ordinary arctangent of the ratio would choose the wrong quadrant. If both arguments vanish, the next weight is zero and its direction is undefined.
These are exact finite-step identities. No assumption about random gradients or equilibrium is needed.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A two-step example exposes the radial memory
text:
A two-step example exposes the radial memory
Use the same normalized predictor and squared loss as Parts 1 and 3. Turn decay off for this example, set \(\eta=1/2\) and \(\beta=0.9\), and begin at \(w_0=(1,0)\).
The first gradient and buffer are \(g_0=m_0=(0,-1)\), so \(w_1=(1,1/2)\). The old gradient is no longer perpendicular to the new weight:
\[
\langle w_1,m_0\rangle=-1/2.
\]
The new gradient is still tangent. Direct differentiation gives
\[
g_1\approx(0.197771,-0.395542),
\qquad
m_1\approx(0.197771,-1.295542).
\]
Since \(R_1=\sqrt5/2\), the radial component is
\[
p_1=\frac{\langle w_1,m_1\rangle}{R_1}
=-\frac{\beta\eta\|m_0\|_2^2}{R_1}
\approx-0.402492.
\]
The equality uses \(m_0\perp w_0\) and \(g_1\perp w_1\). It is a statement about this second step with a zero initial buffer, not a formula for every later \(p_t\).
The tangent component has norm \(\|v_1\|_2\approx1.247214\). The exact geometric formula gives a rotation of approximately \(25.30^\circ\), and the next weight is
\[
w_2\approx(0.901115,1.147771).
\]
Pretending that the whole buffer were tangent would instead give \(\arctan(\eta\|m_1\|_2/R_1)\approx30.37^\circ\).



The second momentum step in the worked example. The current gradient step is tangent, but the contribution from the previous gradient has a radial component. The same total step splits exactly into radial and tangent displacements.


The negative \(p_1\) has a useful interpretation. We subtract the buffer, so its negative radial component adds an outward displacement. The step contains more radial growth than we would infer from a tangent-gradient picture alone.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A unit update does not fix a rotation
text:
A unit update does not fix a rotation
Suppose we normalize a nonzero proposed update \(u\) to length one and apply \(w^+=aw-\eta u\). Set
\[
r=\langle e,u\rangle,
\qquad \|u-r e\|_2=\sqrt{1-r^2}.
\]
When \(aR-\eta r>0\),
\[
\tan\theta
=\frac{\eta\sqrt{1-r^2}}{aR-\eta r}.
\]
For a tangent unit update, \(r=0\) and the familiar ratio is \(\eta/(aR)\). If the update is not tangent, that ratio does not determine the angle.
Take \(w=(1,0)\), \(a=1\), and \(\eta=1/2\). Both \(u=(0,-1)\) and \(\widetilde u=(-0.8,-0.6)\) have unit norm. They produce
\[
w^+=(1,0.5),\qquad
\widetilde w^+=(1.4,0.3),
\]
with rotations \(26.57^\circ\) and \(12.09^\circ\). Both relative displacement lengths are \(1/2\).



Two unit-length update proposals at the same weight and learning rate. Their displacement lengths match, but one rotates the weight by 26.57 degrees and the other by 12.09 degrees.


Normalizing an update controls its length. Removing its radial component is a separate operation. Renormalizing the resulting weight is another: multiplying a nonzero \(w^+\) by a positive scalar does not undo the angle it already acquired.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A rescaled checkpoint also needs a rescaled buffer
text:
A rescaled checkpoint also needs a rescaled buffer
Momentum makes the optimizer state part of any trajectory comparison.
For a constant \(c>0\), an exactly corresponding run under our convention uses
\[
\widetilde w_t=cw_t,
\qquad
\widetilde m_{t-1}=m_{t-1}/c,
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=c^2\eta_t.
\]
Keep \(\beta\) and \(a_t\) the same in both runs. The gradients scale as \(1/c\), so the buffer recurrence preserves \(\widetilde m_t=m_t/c\). The weight recurrence then preserves \(\widetilde w_{t+1}=cw_{t+1}\).
If decay is parameterized by \(a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t\), matching \(a_t\) requires \(\widetilde\lambda_t=\lambda_t/c^2\). Rescaling the learning rate while leaving \(\lambda_t\) fixed would change the shrinkage too.
At a checkpoint, keeping the old buffer unchanged, or resetting it to zero, breaks this correspondence in general. A resulting transient cannot automatically be attributed to the geometry of the represented function.


What becomes of Part 3’s exact clock change?

Keep the cumulative shrinkage \(c_{t+1}=a_tc_t\) and the coordinates \(z_t=w_t/c_t\). For the decoupled convention used here, define \(q_t=c_tm_t\). For \(t\geq1\),
\[
q_t=\beta a_{t-1}q_{t-1}+\nabla L_t(z_t),
\]
and
\[
z_{t+1}=z_t-\frac{\eta_t}{c_tc_{t+1}}q_t.
\]
With the zero initial buffer, \(q_0=\nabla L_0(z_0)\). This is again an exact no-decay representation, but the effective momentum coefficient has changed as well as the learning rate. For constant \(a\), it is \(\beta a\).
The transformation is a direct calculation for our explicitly chosen buffer. It is not the momentum formula from Li and Arora’s coupled-penalty convention. Their Section 2.2 treats that convention with a different full-state transformation.
Copying only the schedule from Part 3 while retaining \(\beta\) would generally compare different trajectories.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: One angle cannot summarize the whole learning process
text:
One angle cannot summarize the whole learning process
Even an exact angle only describes the present directional displacement. Momentum also changes correlations between updates over time. A long sequence of similarly directed rotations can travel differently from a sequence whose rotations cancel, even if their per-step angle magnitudes agree.
Kosson, Messmer, and Jaggi distinguish instantaneous update sizes from longer-term contributions in their rotational-equilibrium analysis. Their predictions use a simplified random-walk model. We have used exact local identities here, rather than importing its equilibrium assumptions.
We now have three quantities to keep track of: the radius, the tangent displacement, and the radial component of the optimizer’s proposal. We also need its memory when comparing trajectories. None of these alone says whether a learned feature became more useful.
The next part of the series turns toward that missing functional measurement: what should count as a small change to a layer when its job is to transform activations?

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Try moving the memory
text:
Try moving the memory

At \(w=(1,0)\), let \(u=(0,-1)\), \(a=0.8\), and \(\eta=0.2\). Compute the new weight and its angle.
With \(w=(1,0)\), \(u=(1,0)\), and \(a=1\), what happens at \(\eta=1\) and \(\eta=2\)? Why is the tangent-ratio formula insufficient?
Double a weight and compare the same represented predictor. How should the unscaled buffer, learning rate, and decay coefficient change under our constant-\(c\) correspondence?
In the expandable clock calculation, use \(a=0.9\) and \(\beta=0.9\). What momentum coefficient does the no-decay \(q\) recurrence use after the first step?



Answer sketches


\(w^+=(0.8,0.2)\) and \(\theta=\arctan(1/4)\approx14.04^\circ\).
At \(\eta=1\), the new weight is zero and its direction is undefined. At \(\eta=2\), it is \((-1,0)\) and the angle is \(180^\circ\). The tangent numerator is zero in both cases, but the radial part distinguishes them.
Divide the buffer by two, multiply the learning rate by four, and divide \(\lambda\) by four, preserving the same shrinkage factor and \(\beta\). Resetting the buffer is a different intervention.
It is \(\beta a=0.81\). This answer depends on the decoupled, unscaled-buffer convention displayed in this post.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Ilya Loshchilov and Frank Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (ICLR 2019), Section 2 and Algorithm 1, distinguishes coupled regularization from decoupled shrinkage. Check both decay placement and whether the buffer stores a gradient or a learning-rate-scaled displacement.
Zhiyuan Li and Sanjeev Arora, An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning (ICLR 2020), Definition 1.2 and Sections 2.2 and 2.3, treats trajectory equivalence with momentum and the required state transformations. Its coupled-penalty convention differs from the decoupled example derived here.
Atli Kosson, Bettina Messmer, and Martin Jaggi, Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks (ICML 2024), Sections 2 and 3.1 and Appendices C and L, connects angular updates, momentum, and total update contributions. The equilibrium estimates require their modeling assumptions. Our worked examples and radial-tangent identities are direct finite-step calculations, not evidence for an optimizer ranking.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: First ask what is being rescaled
text:
First ask what is being rescaled
For a vector \(h\in\mathbb R^d\), define its root mean square by
\[
s(h)=\sqrt{\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2}.
\]
Ignore the stabilizing epsilon for a moment, assume \(h\ne0\), and use the gain-free normalization \(n(h)=h/s(h)\). For \(c>0\),
\[
n(ch)=\frac{ch}{c\,s(h)}=n(h).
\]
Now compare the two compositions:
\[
n(Wx)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Wn(x).
\]
In the first, replacing \(W\) by \(cW\) disappears inside the normalization, provided \(Wx\ne0\) on the inputs under discussion. In the second, it multiplies the output by \(c\).
If the rest of the computation uses \(W\) only through \(n(Wx)\), the first expression gives blockwise scale invariance. If \(W\) has another consumer, that consumer must be checked too. This is a statement about the computation graph, not just a property of a normalization formula.



Normalization after a matrix cancels a common positive matrix scale in the idealized formula. Normalization before a matrix leaves its output scale visible.


The RMSNorm paper by Zhang and Sennrich studies normalization by root mean square. The cancellation above follows directly from its idealized denominator. It should not be read as permission to rescale arbitrary matrices in a model that uses RMSNorm.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: LayerNorm cancels a particular common scale too
text:
LayerNorm cancels a particular common scale too
Write the mean and variance across channels as
\[
\mu(h)=\frac1d\sum_j h_j,
\qquad
v(h)=\frac1d\sum_j(h_j-\mu(h))^2.
\]
The gain-free, zero-epsilon LayerNorm expression is
\[
\ell(h)=\frac{h-\mu(h)\mathbf1}{\sqrt{v(h)}}.
\]
For \(c>0\) and any scalar \(b\), provided \(v(h)>0\),
\[
\ell(ch+b\mathbf1)=\ell(h).
\]
The common shift cancels in the numerator. The common positive scale cancels between numerator and denominator. This does not say that separately rescaling each channel leaves the result unchanged. Such a transformation usually changes both the centered direction and the relative channel magnitudes.
Ba, Kiros, and Hinton’s Layer Normalization paper defines these per-example statistics and examines the associated invariances in Section 5. The axis used to compute the statistics determines what a common rescaling means. BatchNorm uses different statistics, and frozen inference statistics require their own check.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Epsilon makes the ideal identity approximate
text:
Epsilon makes the ideal identity approximate
With a fixed \(\epsilon>0\), the RMS expression becomes
\[
n_\epsilon(h)=\frac{h}{\sqrt{s(h)^2+\epsilon}}.
\]
For positive \(c\),
\[
n_\epsilon(ch)
=\frac{h}{\sqrt{s(h)^2+\epsilon/c^2}}.
\]
This is generally different from \(n_\epsilon(h)\). The approximation is useful when epsilon is negligible relative to the squared activation scale, but the exact symmetry is gone. LayerNorm has the corresponding change from \(\epsilon\) to \(\epsilon/c^2\) after factoring out a common positive scale.
For example, take \(h=(1,2)\), so \(s(h)^2=5/2\). The denominators for \(n_1(h)\) and \(n_1(2h)\), expressed using the same numerator \(h\), are \(\sqrt{7/2}\) and \(\sqrt{11/4}\). They are visibly unequal. The deliberately large epsilon makes the difference easy to see.
An exact theorem needs the exact identity it assumes. A practical approximation needs a scale regime in which the discrepancy is small.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: A learned gain creates a different symmetry
text:
A learned gain creates a different symmetry
Suppose \(z(x)\) already denotes normalized features and the next operation is
\[
f(x)=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x).
\]
The effective linear map is \(A=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)\). Replacing only \(W\) by \(cW\) changes \(A\). Replacing both parameters according to
\[
W\mapsto cW,
\qquad
\gamma\mapsto\gamma/c
\]
preserves \(A\) exactly. This cancellation does not depend on neglecting epsilon because the already-computed features \(z(x)\) are unchanged.
There is redundancy in the pair \((W,\gamma)\), but that is not independent scale invariance of \(W\). The elementary loss
\[
L(w,g)=\frac12(wg-1)^2
\]
makes the distinction concrete. At \((w,g)=(1,1)\) the loss is zero. At \((2,1)\) it is \(1/2\). At \((2,1/2)\) it is zero again. The joint transformation preserves the function. Changing one coordinate alone does not.
If a normalized output also includes a learned additive offset, rescaling the entire downstream matrix requires compensating that offset as well. The displayed identity assumes the bias-free form written above.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Sharing a gain couples its consumers
text:
Sharing a gain couples its consumers
Let two branches consume the same gained features:
\[
f_1(x)=W_1\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x),
\qquad
f_2(x)=W_2\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x).
\]
One gain can compensate a common rescaling of both matrices. If we rescale only \(W_1\) and divide the gain to compensate, we also change the second branch. The bookkeeping is no longer local to one matrix.
The scalar version is enough to expose the issue. Take a nonzero scalar feature \(z\) and require branch outputs \(z\) and \(2z\):
\[
g w_1=1,\qquad g w_2=2.
\]
A shared gain allows many representations, for example \((g,w_1,w_2)=(1,1,2)\) and \((2,1/2,1)\). But requiring both \(|w_1|=1\) and \(|w_2|=1\) makes those two target equations incompatible. Their magnitude ratio must remain two, while the constraints force it to one.
That is a claim about prescribed branch outputs with fixed features and one shared scalar gain. It does not prove that a complete trainable attention network loses an entire class of functions. Other factorizations, later layers, or changing features may compensate. The later research posts will ask which of these freedoms matter.
The useful lesson already holds: the existence of one function-preserving rescaling does not prove that every proposed collection of norm constraints is harmless.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Residual paths keep relative scales visible
text:
Residual paths keep relative scales visible
For a residual expression
\[
y=x+Wn(x),
\]
scaling \(W\) changes the branch relative to the skip path. Even a normalization after the addition does not generally erase that change: the sum’s direction can change rather than only its magnitude.
For a direct example, take \(x=(1,0)\) and a branch output \((0,1)\). The sums \((1,1)\) and \((1,2)\) are not positive scalar multiples of one another. RMS normalization preserves their different directions.
This is why a blanket statement about all matrices in a normalized architecture is too coarse. We need to trace where the scale travels and which quantities meet at each addition, product, or shared parameter.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Three questions before imposing a constraint
text:
Three questions before imposing a constraint
When I see a claim that a weight norm can be fixed without changing the model, I now want three things specified:

Which parameters move, and which remain fixed?
Which output or final function is preserved, under what exact assumptions?
Can all the proposed constraints be satisfied simultaneously by a representative of that function?

The first post explains why a redundant radius can still affect learning. This post identifies where that redundancy actually lives. The next step is to put decay back into the dynamics and distinguish its direct penalty from the training path it induces.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Try the symmetries
text:
Try the symmetries

For \(h=(1,2)\), compare zero-epsilon LayerNorm before and after multiplying only the first channel by three.
In the two-branch scalar example, replace the shared gain by independent gains \(g_1,g_2\). Can both weights now have magnitude one?
For nonzero channel gains, find a channelwise transformation of \(\gamma_j\) and every consuming column \(W_i[:,j]\) that preserves all effective maps.



Answer sketches


The normalized first vector is \((-1,1)\). The transformed vector is \((3,2)\), whose normalized form is \((1,-1)\). Both variances are nonzero, but the direction has changed.
Yes. Take \(w_1=w_2=1\), \(g_1=1\), and \(g_2=2\). The missing relative scale is now a learnable parameter.
For any \(d_j>0\), set \(\gamma_j'=d_j\gamma_j\) and \(W_i'[:,j]=W_i[:,j]/d_j\) for every consumer \(i\). A shared gain requires the compensation at every consuming branch.

text:

Layer Normalization (Ba, Kiros, and Hinton, 2016), especially Section 5, and Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), especially Sections 3 and 4, provide the normalization definitions and invariance context.
L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization (van Laarhoven, 2017) explains why the scope of scale invariance matters for optimization. The placement comparisons, epsilon calculation, and scalar shared-gain example above follow directly from their displayed definitions. They do not establish an empirical optimizer ranking or a full-network expressivity result.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Specify what must be preserved
text:
Specify what must be preserved
Let \(z(x)\in\mathbb R^d\) be fixed features, and let several branches compute
\[
f_i(x)=A_i z(x),\qquad
A_i=W_i\operatorname{diag}(\gamma).
\]
We prescribe the target matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times d}\) and require
\[
\lVert W_i\rVert_F=R_i>0
\]
for every branch. Every gain entry must be finite and nonzero. The question is whether one shared gain vector can represent all those target maps while meeting all the radii.
Preserving each branch map is stronger than preserving the final network function. We keep the stronger requirement visible rather than quietly switching between them.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: The compatibility problem becomes linear
text:
The compatibility problem becomes linear
Define a nonnegative matrix of target column energies and a vector of squared radii:
\[
C_{ij}=\lVert A_i[:,j]\rVert_2^2,
\qquad r_i=R_i^2.
\]
Then the representation exists if and only if
\[
Cq=r\quad\text{for some }q\in(0,\infty)^d.
\]
For necessity, the target identity forces \(W_i[:,j]=A_i[:,j]/\gamma_j\), so
\[
R_i^2=\sum_j\frac{\lVert A_i[:,j]\rVert_2^2}{\gamma_j^2}.
\]
Set \(q_j=\gamma_j^{-2}\). This gives the positive linear system.
For sufficiency, given such a \(q\), choose \(\gamma_j=q_j^{-1/2}\) and \(W_i[:,j]=q_j^{1/2}A_i[:,j]\). The effective maps and every required radius then follow directly.
The criterion uses squared Frobenius lengths. It is not automatically a criterion for spectral or Stiefel constraints. It also excludes zero gain entries, which can hide nonzero weight columns when their target columns vanish.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Two branches make the geometry visible
text:
Two branches make the geometry visible
Assume the first branch has positive column energies \(C_{1j}>0\). For any feasible \(q>0\),
\[
\frac{r_2}{r_1}
=\sum_j\omega_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}},
\qquad
\omega_j=\frac{C_{1j}q_j}{\sum_s C_{1s}q_s}>0,
\quad\sum_j\omega_j=1.
\]
The required squared-radius ratio must be a positive weighted average of the column-energy ratios. If those ratios are not all equal, feasibility is equivalent to
\[
\min_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}}
<\frac{r_2}{r_1}
<\max_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}}.
\]
Conversely, choose strictly positive averaging weights with the required mean and set \(q_j=r_1\omega_j/C_{1j}\). If all energy ratios equal a constant, the required radius ratio must equal that constant too.
Take target rows \(A_1=(1,1)\) and \(A_2=(1,2)\). Then
\[
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The squared-radius vector \(r=(2,4)\) is feasible, with \(q=(4/3,2/3)\). The gain magnitudes are approximately \((0.866025,1.224745)\).
The boundary target \(r=(2,2)\) would require \(q_2=0\). It is not feasible with a finite nonzero second gain. Allowing nonnegative coefficients can therefore admit limits that the original parameterization does not attain.



Positive combinations of the column-energy vectors one-one and one-four fill the open wedge between their rays. The target squared radii two-four lies inside. Two-two is on the excluded boundary, and two-ten lies outside.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Finite gain bounds impose more than formal feasibility
text:
Finite gain bounds impose more than formal feasibility
If \(0<g_{\min}\leq|\gamma_j|\leq g_{\max}<\infty\), then the exact condition becomes
\[
Cq=r,\qquad
g_{\max}^{-2}\leq q_j\leq g_{\min}^{-2}.
\]
This is a box-constrained linear feasibility problem. A representation can exist in principle while requiring gain magnitudes outside a chosen stable range.
In the example above, restricting both gain magnitudes to \([1,2]\) forces \(q_j\in[1/4,1]\). The first equation \(q_1+q_2=2\) then forces both coefficients to one, making the second equation equal five rather than four. The formally feasible target is no longer feasible under these gain bounds.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: A proportional pair is incompatible at equal radii
text:
A proportional pair is incompatible at equal radii
If \(A_2=2A_1\ne0\), then \(C_{2j}=4C_{1j}\) for every column. Any shared-gain representation must satisfy \(r_2=4r_1\).
Equal imposed radii contradict that requirement. Increasing the number of columns does not repair this particular obstruction while the target relation \(A_2=2A_1\) is preserved.
That is an exact local statement. Learned upstream features, independent branch multipliers, or other function-preserving transformations can change the question. They are not included in this prescribed-map criterion.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: A scalar gain gives an exact fitting floor
text:
A scalar gain gives an exact fitting floor
Now use one shared scalar \(g\geq0\) instead of a channelwise vector. Assume fixed features satisfy \(\mathbb E[zz^\top]=I\), and supervise all branch outputs with targets \(A_i z\). The population loss is
\[
\mathcal L(g,W)=\frac12\sum_i\lVert gW_i-A_i\rVert_F^2,
\qquad \lVert W_i\rVert_F=R_i.
\]
Write \(b_i=\lVert A_i\rVert_F>0\). For a fixed positive \(g\), Cauchy-Schwarz shows that an optimal \(W_i\) aligns with its target, giving
\[
\min_W\mathcal L(g,W)=\frac12\sum_i(gR_i-b_i)^2.
\]
Minimizing this scalar quadratic yields
\[
g_* =\frac{\sum_iR_ib_i}{\sum_iR_i^2},
\]
\[
\mathcal L_* =\frac12\left(\sum_i b_i^2
-\frac{(\sum_iR_ib_i)^2}{\sum_iR_i^2}\right).
\]
The floor vanishes exactly when the target norm vector is proportional to the radius vector. For \(R=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,2)\), the optimal gain is \(3/2\) and the minimum loss is \(1/4\).
No learning-rate correction can remove a global fitting floor inside this model. The formula does not say that every optimizer reaches the optimum, or that an end-to-end attention task has this same floor.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Grouping changes the feasible set
text:
Grouping changes the feasible set
Replace the individual radii with a joint constraint
\[
\sum_i\lVert W_i\rVert_F^2=R^2.
\]
For any nonzero target tuple, choose
\[
g=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_i\lVert A_i\rVert_F^2}}{R},
\qquad W_i=A_i/g.
\]
All target maps are preserved and the joint constraint holds. Independent learned branch multipliers provide another way to restore the missing amplitude freedom.
The distinction is which scales the constraint fixes. Individual radii fix relative branch norms as well as total scale. A group radius leaves those relative norms available.
The next post asks whether this local obstruction predicts a failure in a real module. Before making that claim, we need to let attention use its own factorization freedoms and run controls that could overturn the proposed explanation.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Try the compatibility test
text:
Try the compatibility test

Verify \(Cq=(2,4)\) for the example’s \(q=(4/3,2/3)\).
If \(A_2=3A_1\ne0\), what ratio \(R_2/R_1\) is necessary under a shared gain?
In the scalar-gain model, take \(R=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,3)\). Find the optimum and fitting floor.



Answer sketches


The row sums are \(4/3+2/3=2\) and \(4/3+4(2/3)=4\).
Squared energies scale by nine, so \(R_2/R_1=3\).
\(g_*=2\) and \(\mathcal L_*=[(2-1)^2+(2-3)^2]/2=1\).

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
The cone criterion and scalar fitting-floor calculation are elementary derivations from the displayed model. They are not claims of publication priority or a theorem about a full trainable Transformer.
Hyperball Optimization, Section 4.1, gives the matrix-and-gain rescaling that motivates asking whether several constraints are compatible. Learnable Multipliers, Sections 2 and 4.1 and Appendix C, supplies established multiplier and symmetry baselines. Neither citation substitutes for checking the exact consumers and constraints in a proposed application.

title: The same network, a different step
section: A predictor that forgets its radius
text:
A predictor that forgets its radius
Let \(w\in\mathbb R^2\) be nonzero and define
\[
f_w(x)=\frac{w^\top x}{\|w\|_2}.
\]
For every positive \(c\), \(f_{cw}(x)=f_w(x)\). The predictor remembers the direction of \(w\) and forgets its length. The restriction \(c>0\) matters: a negative multiplier reverses the prediction.
Write \(w=Re\), where \(R=\|w\|_2>0\) and \(\|e\|_2=1\). All points on the positive ray through \(e\) describe the same function. The parameter vector has two coordinates, but this predictor has only one directional degree of freedom.
For a fixed dataset, any differentiable loss built only from these predictions satisfies
\[
L(cw)=L(w).
\]
This is an assumption about a particular parameter block with everything else fixed. We will spend the next post checking when normalization actually gives us this assumption.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Two derivatives tell us what SGD sees
text:
Two derivatives tell us what SGD sees
Differentiate \(L(cw)=L(w)\) with respect to \(c\) at \(c=1\):
\[
\langle w,\nabla L(w)\rangle=0.
\]
The gradient is perpendicular to the weight. Moving directly along the ray has zero first-order effect on the loss, so the gradient has no radial component.
Next differentiate the same identity with respect to \(w\), holding \(c\) fixed. The chain rule gives
\[
c\nabla L(cw)=\nabla L(w).
\]
Doubling the weight therefore halves its gradient. These are standard scale-invariance identities. Their implication for effective learning rates is developed in van Laarhoven’s analysis of regularization and normalization, especially Section 3.1.
Let \(g(e)=\nabla L(e)\). Since \(\nabla L(Re)=g(e)/R\), one raw SGD step is
\[
w^+=Re-\frac{\eta}{R}g(e)
=R\left(e-\frac{\eta}{R^2}g(e)\right).
\]
The outside factor \(R\) does not affect our predictor. The directional change is governed by \(\eta/R^2\), rather than \(\eta\) alone.
One factor of \(1/R\) comes from the smaller gradient. The other comes from comparing that displacement with a longer weight vector.

title: The same network, a different step
section: One exact step, with numbers
text:
One exact step, with numbers
Use the single input \(x=(0,1)\), target \(1\), and squared loss
\[
L(w)=\frac12\left(\frac{w_2}{\sqrt{w_1^2+w_2^2}}-1\right)^2.
\]
Start one copy at \(w=(1,0)\) and another at \(\widetilde w=(2,0)\). Both predict zero and have loss \(1/2\). Their gradients are
\[
\nabla L(1,0)=(0,-1),
\qquad
\nabla L(2,0)=(0,-1/2).
\]
With the same learning rate \(\eta=1/2\), the updated weights are
\[
w^+=(1,1/2),\qquad
\widetilde w^+=(2,1/4).
\]
Their slopes are \(1/2\) and \(1/8\). The rotation angles are approximately \(26.57^\circ\) and \(7.13^\circ\). Their new predictions are \(1/\sqrt5\approx0.4472\) and \(1/\sqrt{65}\approx0.1240\).



Two SGD steps from equivalent predictors. At radius one the tangent step is one half and the rotation is 26.57 degrees. At radius two the tangent step is one quarter and the rotation is 7.13 degrees.


The second copy moved less in parameter space and started farther from the origin. Both effects reduced its rotation. The initial function was identical, but the optimizer did not treat the two representations identically.
To recover the first copy’s new direction, the second copy would need learning rate \(2\), four times as large. That statement concerns this corresponding step. Maintaining equivalence through a whole run requires tracking how radii and optimizer states evolve.

title: The same network, a different step
section: The angle is exact, the effective step is local
text:
The angle is exact, the effective step is local
Because \(g(e)\) is perpendicular to \(e\), the angle \(\theta\) between \(w\) and \(w^+\) obeys
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{\eta\|g(e)\|_2}{R^2}.
\]
This is an exact finite-step identity for the stated update. Calling \(\eta/R^2\) an effective learning rate describes the coefficient in the normalized directional update. It is not a claim that the angle equals that coefficient for a large step.
The next radius also changes:
\[
\|w^+\|_2^2
=R^2+\frac{\eta^2}{R^2}\|g(e)\|_2^2.
\]
A tangent displacement leaves the radius unchanged to first order, but a finite tangent step ends outside the original circle. Repeated SGD steps can grow the radius and thereby change subsequent directional steps. We do not need an equilibrium approximation to see this feedback.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Where weight decay will enter
text:
Where weight decay will enter
For the update convention
\[
w^+=(1-\eta\lambda)w-\eta\nabla L(w),
\]
assume \(1-\eta\lambda>0\). The decay term shortens the radial part while the gradient remains tangent. The same right triangle now gives
\[
\tan\theta
=\frac{\eta\|g(e)\|_2}{(1-\eta\lambda)R^2}.
\]
Decay alone preserves the predictor in this model, but decay inside a training update can alter the direction learned next. This is the first reason to be suspicious of the phrase “scale does not matter.”
The equation is for raw SGD with this decay convention. With momentum, the accumulated update need not remain tangent to the current weight. With a normalized update, the displacement need not shrink as \(1/R\). We will derive those cases separately rather than reuse the SGD formula.
An angular change is also not a universal measure of progress. Our example changes one prediction by a known amount. In a large network, a rotation could help, hurt, or barely affect the output.

title: The same network, a different step
section: The coordinates we choose become part of learning
text:
The coordinates we choose become part of learning
The example isolates three different objects: the function, its redundant parameter representation, and the rule that moves that representation. Equality of the first does not imply equality of the third.
That distinction will connect the rest of this series. Weight decay changes radii. Normalization determines which rescalings preserve a function. Layer norms specify which perturbations count as small. Modula combines those local choices into a network geometry. Before choosing any constraint, we need to know which of these scales it controls.
The next post asks where the exact symmetry comes from, and why normalizing the input to a matrix does not usually make that matrix’s own scale disappear.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Try the calculation
text:
Try the calculation

Start a third copy at \((3,0)\). What learning rate makes its first updated direction agree with the radius-one copy using \(\eta=1/2\)?
Use the unit update \(u=\nabla L(w)/\|\nabla L(w)\|_2\) instead of the raw gradient. What is \(\tan\theta\) when the gradient is nonzero?
Why can a tangent step increase the radius even though the directional derivative of the squared radius is zero?



Answer sketches


The coefficient \(\eta/R^2\) must equal \(1/2\), so \(\eta=9/2\).
The displacement has length \(\eta\) and is perpendicular to \(w\), so \(\tan\theta=\eta/R\). The squared-radius law for raw SGD no longer applies to this normalized update.
Expanding the squared norm gives the zero first-order cross term plus the positive second-order term \(\eta^2\|\nabla L(w)\|_2^2\).

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Put the product in a positive form
text:
Put the product in a positive form
For positive semidefinite \(A,B\), use \[
P=A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}.
\] It is positive semidefinite because \[
x^*Px=(A^{1/2}x)^*B(A^{1/2}x)\geq0.
\] Cyclicity gives \[
\operatorname{Tr}(P^k)=\operatorname{Tr}((AB)^k).
\] For invertible \(A\), the matrices are similar: \[
A^{-1/2}(AB)A^{1/2}=A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}.
\] For singular \(A\), the determinant identity \(\det(I-tXY)=\det(I-tYX)\) still gives the same characteristic polynomial, with \(X=A^{1/2}\) and \(Y=A^{1/2}B\). Nevertheless, the positive representative is preferable for spectral analysis and numerical eigensolvers.
For bounded positive free variables \(a,b\) in a tracial operator-algebra setting, the law of \(a^{1/2}ba^{1/2}\) is called multiplicative free convolution, written \[
\mu_a\boxtimes\mu_b.
\] It is determined by the marginal laws and freeness. Our assumptions of positivity and boundedness make the law and square root unambiguous.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: The first two product moments
text:
The first two product moments
Let \(\alpha=\tau(a)\) and \(\beta=\tau(b)\). Freeness gives \[
\tau(ab)=\alpha\beta.
\] Write \(a=\alpha1+a_0\), \(b=\beta1+b_0\), where the subscripted variables are centered. Expanding \(abab\), terms with one centered factor vanish. Terms with two centered factors survive only when they use the same variable. The terms with three centered factors vanish by freeness and cyclicity, and \(\tau(a_0b_0a_0b_0)=0\).
Therefore \[
\begin{aligned}
\tau(abab)
&=\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\tau(a_0^2)+\alpha^2\tau(b_0^2)\\
&=\beta^2m_2(a)+\alpha^2m_2(b)-\alpha^2\beta^2.
\end{aligned}
\] For mean-one variables with variances \(v_a,v_b\), the product has mean one and variance \(v_a+v_b\).
Classically independent positive variables instead give \(\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]=\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Y^2]\), hence variance \(v_a+v_b+v_av_b\) when both means are one. The same two marginal spectra can produce a different second product moment depending on how their directions interact.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Build the S-transform
text:
Build the S-transform
Define the moment series without its constant term: \[
\psi_\mu(t)=\int\frac{tx}{1-tx}\,d\mu(x)
=\sum_{k\geq1}m_kt^k.
\] Assume \(m_1\neq0\). Since \(\psi_\mu'(0)=m_1\), it has a local compositional inverse \(\chi_\mu\) near zero. Set \[
\boxed{S_\mu(w)=\frac{1+w}{w}\chi_\mu(w).}
\] The apparent singularity at zero is removable. Because \(\chi(w)=w/m_1+O(w^2)\), \[
S_\mu(0)=\frac1{m_1}.
\] For a positive law, the only zero-mean case is \(\delta_0\), whose product law is trivially \(\delta_0\). A centered sign variable, however, does not have this ordinary S-transform: its moment series has no linear term. We cannot reuse the sign example without changing the setup.
The multiplicative analogue of R-transform additivity is the theorem \[
\boxed{S_{\mu\boxtimes\nu}(w)=S_\mu(w)S_\nu(w).}
\] This is a substantive theorem about free products, not a consequence of the inverse-function definition alone. Its combinatorial proof uses noncrossing partitions and their complements. See Nica and Speicher, Lectures 14 and 18.
A short expansion connects it to our earlier calculation. Inverting \(\psi(t)=m_1t+m_2t^2+\cdots\) gives \[
S(w)=\frac1{m_1}
+\left(\frac1{m_1}-\frac{m_2}{m_1^3}\right)w+O(w^2).
\] For mean-one laws this is \(1-vw+O(w^2)\). Multiplying the two series adds their variances, exactly as the direct mixed-moment calculation predicted.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Checking the S-transform normalization
text:
Checking the S-transform normalization
For a constant \(c>0\), \[
\psi(t)=\frac{ct}{1-ct},\quad
\chi(w)=\frac{w}{c(1+w)},\quad
S_{\delta_c}(w)=\frac1c.
\] Thus multiplying by a constant rescales the law and divides its S-transform by that constant.
For a projection \(p=p^*=p^2\) with \(\tau(p)=\alpha>0\), every positive-order moment is \(\alpha\). Its law is \((1-\alpha)\delta_0+\alpha\delta_1\), so \[
\psi_p(t)=\frac{\alpha t}{1-t},\quad
\chi_p(w)=\frac{w}{\alpha+w},\quad
\boxed{S_p(w)=\frac{1+w}{\alpha+w}.}
\] If \(q\) is a free projection with trace \(\beta>0\), then \[
S_{pqp}(w)=\frac{(1+w)^2}{(\alpha+w)(\beta+w)}.
\] Although \(p\) and \(q\) are projections, \(pqp\) generally is not. Randomly oriented subspaces produce intermediate eigenvalues between zero and one.
Its first two moments, using the calculation above, are \[
m_1=\alpha\beta,\qquad
m_2=\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta-\alpha\beta).
\] At \(\alpha=\beta=1/2\), these are \(1/4\) and \(3/16\). An intersection indicator for independent commuting scalar events would instead have both moments equal to \(1/4\). This gives a concrete distinction between multiplying free projections and multiplying independent indicator variables.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Recovering a law from its S-transform
text:
Recovering a law from its S-transform
Use the same Cauchy-transform convention as Part III. Then \[
\psi(1/z)=zG(z)-1.
\] Writing \(w=zG(z)-1\), the inverse relation is \(\chi(w)=1/z\). Substituting into the S-transform definition gives \[
\boxed{zwS(w)=1+w,\qquad G(z)=\frac{1+w}{z}.}
\] Choose the solution with \(w\to0\) as \(z\to\infty\) and the correct upper-half-plane behavior for \(G\). This is the computational route we will use for covariance products in the final post.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

What is \(S_{\delta_1}\), and why is that necessary?
Show directly that \(S_{ca}(w)=S_a(w)/c\) for \(c>0\).
If two free positive mean-one variables each have second moment two, what is the second moment of their product?



Answer sketches


It is one, the multiplicative identity. Multiplying by the identity operator must preserve the law.
\(\psi_{ca}(t)=\psi_a(ct)\), so the compositional inverse is \(\chi_a(w)/c\).
Each variance is one. The product variance is two and its mean is one, so its second moment is three.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: The Cauchy transform
text:
The Cauchy transform
For a compactly supported probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R\), define its Cauchy transform by \[
G_\mu(z)=\int\frac{1}{z-x}\,d\mu(x),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.
\] Our sign convention matters. With \(1/(z-x)\), the imaginary part of \(G\) is negative in the upper half-plane. Some references use the negative of this transform.
For sufficiently large \(|z|\), expand the geometric series: \[
G_\mu(z)=\frac1z+\frac{m_1}{z^2}+\frac{m_2}{z^3}+\cdots.
\] Thus \(G\) encodes every moment, and its leading behavior must be \(1/z\).
It also recovers the density. Indeed, \[
-\frac1\pi\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(x+i\eta)
=\int\frac{\eta}{\pi((x-t)^2+\eta^2)}\,d\mu(t).
\] The right side smooths the measure with a Cauchy kernel. At continuity points of a density \(\rho\), letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) gives \(\rho(x)\). More generally, Stieltjes inversion recovers masses of intervals. An atom at \(x_0\) can be checked separately through \[
\mu(\{x_0\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}i\eta G_\mu(x_0+i\eta).
\]

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: From the moment formula to a functional equation
text:
From the moment formula to a functional equation
Introduce the two generating series \[
M(t)=1+\sum_{n\geq1}m_nt^n,
\qquad R(w)=\sum_{n\geq1}\kappa_nw^{n-1}.
\] Look at the block containing position 1 in a noncrossing partition. If that block has size \(k\), it leaves \(k\) ordered gaps, each carrying an independent noncrossing partition. This decomposes the moment formula into \[
M(t)=1+\sum_{k\geq1}\kappa_k t^kM(t)^k
=1+tM(t)R(tM(t)).
\] Since \(G(z)=z^{-1}M(z^{-1})\), substitution gives \[
zG(z)=1+G(z)R(G(z)),
\] or \[
\boxed{z=\frac1{G(z)}+R(G(z)).}
\] Initially this identity holds near infinity, or as a formal Laurent-series identity. We should not assume that the power series for \(R\) converges at every value of \(G\).
Equivalently, let \(K\) denote the local compositional inverse of \(G\) near infinity, so \(K(w)\sim1/w\) near zero. Then \[
R(w)=K(w)-\frac1w.
\] This is the R-transform. Cumulant additivity becomes \[
\boxed{R_{\mu\boxplus\nu}(w)=R_\mu(w)+R_\nu(w).}
\] The local inverse and analytic extension are developed rigorously in Speicher, Theorem 4.12.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Warm-up: adding semicircles
text:
Warm-up: adding semicircles
A centered semicircular variable of variance \(v\) has only one nonzero cumulant, \(\kappa_2=v\). Therefore \(R(w)=vw\) and \[
vG(z)^2-zG(z)+1=0.
\] For \(v>0\), choose the solution \[
G(z)=\frac{z-\sqrt{z^2-4v}}{2v},
\] where the square root is the branch asymptotic to \(z\) at infinity. The other solution grows like \(z/v\), which cannot be the transform of a probability measure.
Taking the boundary value in the upper half-plane recovers the semicircle density. Adding free semicircles of variances \(v_1,v_2\) simply replaces \(vw\) by \((v_1+v_2)w\). Their sum is semicircular with variance \(v_1+v_2\).

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Adding two free sign variables
text:
Adding two free sign variables
Let \(\mu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1\). Its transform is immediate: \[
G_\mu(z)=\frac12\left(\frac1{z-1}+\frac1{z+1}\right)
=\frac{z}{z^2-1}.
\] Solve \(w=z/(z^2-1)\) for \(z\): \[
z=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4w^2}}{2w}.
\] The inverse with a \(1/w\) pole uses the plus sign, with the square root analytic and equal to one at \(w=0\). Hence \[
R_\mu(w)=\frac{\sqrt{1+4w^2}-1}{2w}.
\] Expanding gives \(R_\mu(w)=w-w^3+2w^5-\cdots\), consistent with \(\kappa_2=1\) and \(\kappa_4=-1\).
For \(\nu=\mu\boxplus\mu\), add the two R-transforms. The equation for \(G_\nu\) becomes \[
z=\frac1{G_\nu(z)}+
\frac{\sqrt{1+4G_\nu(z)^2}-1}{G_\nu(z)}
=\frac{\sqrt{1+4G_\nu(z)^2}}{G_\nu(z)}.
\] Squaring yields \((z^2-4)G_\nu(z)^2=1\). Choose the branch matching \(G_\nu(z)\sim1/z\): \[
\boxed{G_\nu(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{z^2-4}}.}
\] Here \(\sqrt{z^2-4}\) means the analytic branch on \(\mathbb C\setminus[-2,2]\) asymptotic to \(z\). It is not the pointwise principal square root of \(z^2-4\) everywhere. The formula agrees with the transform near infinity and continues analytically to the upper half-plane.
For \(-2<x<2\), its boundary value is \[
G_\nu(x+i0)=-\frac{i}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}.
\] Therefore the answer is the arcsine law: \[
\boxed{d\nu(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_{(-2,2)}(x)}{\pi\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx.}
\] The density diverges at the endpoints, but its integral is one. These integrable divergences are not atoms: multiplying the transform by \(i\eta\) at either endpoint gives zero in the limit.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Checking the moments
text:
Checking the moments
Set \(x=2\cos\theta\). The arcsine measure becomes uniform \(d\theta/\pi\) on \([0,\pi]\), so \[
\int x^2\,d\nu(x)=2,\qquad
\int x^4\,d\nu(x)=6.
\] More generally, its odd moments vanish and its \(2k\)th moment is \(\binom{2k}{k}\). This agrees with our mixed-word calculations.
Two free sign variables produce an arcsine law. Many free sign variables, summed and divided by the square root of their number, approach a semicircle. These are different questions, so there is no conflict between the two answers.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Find \(R_{\delta_c}\).
Derive the transform rule for \(ca\) from cumulant scaling.
Why is solving a polynomial equation for \(G\) insufficient without a branch condition?



Answer sketches


\(G(z)=1/(z-c)\), so \(K(w)=c+1/w\) and \(R(w)=c\). Free addition of a constant translates the law.
\(R_{ca}(w)=cR_a(cw)\), since the \(n\)th cumulant scales by \(c^n\).
A polynomial may have several solutions. A probability Cauchy transform must be analytic in the upper half-plane, have negative imaginary part there, and behave like \(1/z\) at infinity. Squaring can introduce extraneous branches.

section: Further reading
text:

Speicher’s lecture notes, Section 4 contain the analytic R-transform theory and the symmetric two-point example. Tao’s free probability notes give another route from transforms to free convolution. Check the sign convention when moving between references.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Eigenvalues are not enough
text:
Eigenvalues are not enough
Take \[
A=B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Both choices of \(B\) have spectrum \(\{-1,1\}\). Nevertheless, \[
\operatorname{spec}(A+B_1)=\{-2,2\},\qquad
\operatorname{spec}(A+B_2)=\{0,0\}.
\] The individual spectra have lost the information about which directions line up.
Writing \(A=U\Lambda U^*\) and \(B=V\Gamma V^*\) makes the missing ingredient explicit: the spectrum of their sum depends on the relative basis \(U^*V\).
Here is a useful replacement for choosing an alignment. Keep deterministic diagonal matrices \(D_n,E_n\), draw a Haar unitary \(U_n\), and study \[
D_n+U_nE_nU_n^*.
\] Haar measure is the uniform probability measure on the unitary group, in the precise sense of invariance under multiplication by any fixed unitary. Conjugation preserves the spectrum of \(E_n\) and randomizes its eigenbasis.
Under suitable hypotheses, this produces a limiting rule for mixed moments. That rule is freeness.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: The trace turns a matrix into a distribution
text:
The trace turns a matrix into a distribution
Define the empirical spectral measure and normalized trace by \[
\mu_A=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_j(A)},
\qquad \tau_n(A)=\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(A).
\] Then \[
\boxed{\tau_n(A^k)=\int x^k\,d\mu_A(x).}
\] A normalized trace of a power is exactly a spectral moment. The normalization gives total mass one, so moments remain comparable as the dimension changes.
To study the sum, expand \(\tau_n((A+B)^k)\). Now words such as \(AABB\) and \(ABAB\) appear. They cannot generally be rearranged into each other. Trace is cyclic, so \(\tau(ABBA)=\tau(AABB)\), but it does not permit arbitrary permutations.
For a random matrix, \(\tau_n(A^k)\) is itself random. Its ensemble average is \(\mathbb E[\tau_n(A^k)]\). We will distinguish these when discussing experiments and convergence.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Noncommutative probability
text:
Noncommutative probability
Our setting is a unital algebra \(\mathcal A\) with an adjoint operation and a normalized positive trace \(\tau\). Thus \(\tau\) is linear and satisfies \[
\tau(1)=1,\qquad \tau(x^*x)\geq0,\qquad \tau(xy)=\tau(yx).
\] Matrices with normalized trace are the finite-dimensional example. For bounded self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem gives a probability law whose moments are \(\tau(a^k)\). We use compactly supported laws throughout the series, so their moments determine them uniquely.
Think of a self-adjoint element \(a=a^*\) as a real random variable and \(\tau\) as expectation. Multiplication may fail to commute, but positivity and spectral measures remain available.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Freeness is a rule for centered, alternating products
text:
Freeness is a rule for centered, alternating products
Unital subalgebras \(\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2,\ldots\) are free if \[
\tau(x_1x_2\cdots x_m)=0
\] whenever each \(x_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal A_{j_i}\), consecutive indices differ, and every factor is centered: \[
j_i\neq j_{i+1},\qquad \tau(x_i)=0.
\] We call \(a\) and \(b\) free when the unital algebras they generate are free. The condition therefore applies to centered polynomials in \(a\) and \(b\), not merely to the original variables.
Why center? Because every factor can be split into its mean and its fluctuation. Expanding these splits reduces mixed moments to simpler ones until the alternating-centered rule applies. This recursively determines the joint moments from the two marginal moment sequences.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: A fourth-moment calculation
text:
A fourth-moment calculation
Suppose \(a,b\) are centered and free, with \[
\tau(a^2)=\alpha,\qquad \tau(b^2)=\beta.
\] The definition immediately gives \[
\tau(ab)=0,\qquad \tau(abab)=0.
\] But \(a^2b^2\) is different. Center the squares: \[
0=\tau\bigl((a^2-\alpha1)(b^2-\beta1)\bigr)
  =\tau(a^2b^2)-\alpha\beta.
\] Consequently, \[
\boxed{\tau(a^2b^2)=\alpha\beta,\qquad \tau(abab)=0.}
\] For centered, classically independent scalar variables \(X,Y\) with those variances, both corresponding expressions equal \(\alpha\beta\), since \(XYXY=X^2Y^2\).
At second order, both theories give variance addition. At fourth order, the distinction becomes visible: \[
\tau((a+b)^4)=\tau(a^4)+\tau(b^4)+4\alpha\beta.
\] To see the coefficient four, list the six words containing two of each letter. The words \(aabb,abba,baab,bbaa\) each contribute \(\alpha\beta\). The alternating words \(abab,baba\) vanish. Words with three of one letter and one of the other also vanish, by centering and cyclicity.
Classical independence instead gives a coefficient of six.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Adding two free sign variables
text:
Adding two free sign variables
Let both marginal laws be \[
\mu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1.
\] Each variable is centered, with second and fourth moments equal to one. The free sum therefore has \[
m_2=2,\qquad m_4=6.
\] The classical sum has masses \(1/4,1/2,1/4\) at \(-2,0,2\), and fourth moment eight. Perfect alignment, where \(b=a\), gives fourth moment sixteen.
We write the law of a free sum as \(\mu\boxplus\nu\), the additive free convolution. Part III will calculate the entire law in this example. Part IV will compare all three eigenbasis choices numerically.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Asymptotic freeness of random matrices
text:
Asymptotic freeness of random matrices
One sufficient setting is that \(D_n,E_n\) are deterministic Hermitian matrices with uniformly bounded operator norms and convergent empirical spectral measures. If \(U_n\) is Haar unitary, then the pair \((D_n,U_nE_nU_n^*)\) converges in joint normalized-trace moments to a free pair, in probability. This is a standard asymptotic-freeness theorem, not something implied just by our definition. Speicher, Section 7.
At each finite dimension, the pair generally fails exact freeness. The theorem describes the limit for each fixed word. Independent random diagonal sign matrices illustrate why ordinary independence alone is insufficient: they commute, and their alternating fourth moment is identically one.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Compute \(\tau((a+b)^2)\) for centered free variables of variances \(\alpha,\beta\).
For the symmetric two-point laws above, compute \(\tau((a+b)^3)\).
Explain why the identity \(a^2=b^2=1\) is compatible with \(\tau(abab)=0\).



Answer sketches


The cross terms vanish, leaving \(\alpha+\beta\).
It is zero. The pure cubic moments vanish by symmetry, and the mixed terms vanish by freeness and cyclicity.
The squares only simplify adjacent equal factors. Simplifying \(abab\) to \(a^2b^2\) would require commutativity.

text:

Terence Tao’s Notes 5 develop the probability-space viewpoint and mixed-moment examples. Speicher’s lecture notes give the definitions in Section 1 and the random-matrix connection in Section 7. The worked calculations here use the conventions stated above.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Crossing and noncrossing partitions
text:
Crossing and noncrossing partitions
A partition divides \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into disjoint nonempty blocks. It is noncrossing if there are no indices \(i<j<k<\ell\) with \(i,k\) in one block and \(j,\ell\) in a different block.
For four positions, the three pairings are \[
\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\},\quad
\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\},\quad
\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}.
\] Only the last one crosses when the positions are placed around a circle.



Two noncrossing pairings and the crossing pairing on four cyclically ordered positions.


For \(abab\), pairing equal letters requires precisely the crossing pairing. For \(aabb\), it requires the first noncrossing pairing. This is the diagrammatic trace of our earlier calculation. To make it a general method, we introduce cumulants.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Cumulants are defined recursively from moments
text:
Cumulants are defined recursively from moments
Write \(NC(n)\) for the set of noncrossing partitions of \(n\) positions. The free cumulants \(\kappa_n\) are the multilinear functionals defined by \[
\tau(x_1\cdots x_n)
=\sum_{\pi\in NC(n)}\kappa_\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_n),
\] where \[
\kappa_\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=\prod_{V\in\pi}\kappa_{|V|}(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_{|V|}}),
\qquad V=\{i_1<\cdots<i_{|V|}\}.
\] The factors on the right are scalars, so their product commutes. Within each cumulant, the original order of the arguments is retained.
This is a recursive definition: the one-block partition contributes \(\kappa_n\), and all other blocks have smaller size. Once cumulants of lower orders are known, solve for \(\kappa_n\).
For one variable, abbreviate \(m_n=\tau(a^n)\) and \(\kappa_n=\kappa_n(a,\ldots,a)\). The first relations are \[
\begin{aligned}
m_1&=\kappa_1,\\
m_2&=\kappa_2+\kappa_1^2,\\
m_3&=\kappa_3+3\kappa_2\kappa_1+\kappa_1^3,\\
m_4&=\kappa_4+4\kappa_3\kappa_1+2\kappa_2^2
       +6\kappa_2\kappa_1^2+\kappa_1^4.
\end{aligned}
\] That coefficient two counts the noncrossing pairings on four positions. Classical cumulants use all set partitions, so the corresponding coefficient is three.
For a centered variable, \[
\kappa_2=m_2,\qquad \kappa_3=m_3,\qquad
\boxed{\kappa_4=m_4-2m_2^2.}
\] For a symmetric sign variable, \(m_2=m_4=1\), giving \(\kappa_4=-1\). A negative fourth free cumulant is entirely possible.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Mixed free cumulants vanish
text:
Mixed free cumulants vanish
The crucial result is the mixed-cumulant characterization of freeness: unital subalgebras are free exactly when every mixed free cumulant vanishes. Here mixed means that its arguments come from more than one of the subalgebras. Speicher, Section 3.
This theorem connects the combinatorial definition to the alternating-centered definition. We use it here without reproducing its full induction proof.
For centered free \(a,b\), apply the moment formula to \(abab\). Singleton blocks vanish by centering. Blocks containing both letters vanish by the theorem. Pairing equal letters would cross. Every contribution is therefore zero.
Now expand a cumulant of \(a+b\) by multilinearity. Every mixed choice of arguments vanishes, leaving only the all-\(a\) and all-\(b\) terms: \[
\boxed{\kappa_n(a+b)=\kappa_n(a)+\kappa_n(b).}
\] The full moment sequence does not add. The cumulant sequence does.
For the sum of two free symmetric sign variables, the second cumulant is two and the fourth is minus two. Hence \[
m_4=-2+2(2)^2=6,
\] recovering Part I without listing sixteen words.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Semicircle moments count noncrossing pairings
text:
Semicircle moments count noncrossing pairings
Suppose \(s\) has cumulants \[
\kappa_1(s)=0,\quad \kappa_2(s)=v,\quad
\kappa_n(s)=0\quad(n\geq3).
\] Only partitions into pairs survive. Odd moments vanish, and \[
\tau(s^{2k})=C_kv^k,
\qquad C_k=\frac1{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}.
\] Why Catalan numbers? Pair the first position with position \(2j+2\). Noncrossing forces the \(2j\) positions inside that pair and the remaining positions outside it to pair separately. If \(C_0=1\), this gives \[
C_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}C_jC_{k-1-j}.
\] Thus the even moments begin \(1,v,2v^2,5v^3,14v^4\) when the initial one is the zeroth moment.
For \(v>0\), these are the moments of the semicircle density \[
\rho_v(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4v-x^2}}{2\pi v}
\,\mathbf1_{\{|x|\leq2\sqrt v\}}.
\] The substitution \(x=2\sqrt v\cos\theta\) verifies the moments by a beta integral. In particular, its variance is \(v\), and its fourth moment is \(2v^2\). When \(v=0\), the law is \(\delta_0\).

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Why a free central limit theorem follows
text:
Why a free central limit theorem follows
Let \(a_1,a_2,\ldots\) be freely independent, identically distributed, bounded self-adjoint variables, centered with variance \(v\). Set \[
s_N=\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_N}{\sqrt N}.
\] Multilinearity gives \(\kappa_k(ca)=c^k\kappa_k(a)\). Additivity then yields \[
\kappa_k(s_N)=N^{1-k/2}\kappa_k(a_1).
\] The first cumulant is zero, the second remains \(v\), and every fixed higher cumulant tends to zero. Since each fixed moment is a finite polynomial in cumulants, the moments converge to those of the semicircle law.
This also gives weak convergence of the laws. The common second moment ensures tightness. Convergence of higher even moments controls the tails needed to pass moments to any weak subsequential limit. The compactly supported semicircle law is moment-determinate, so every such limit is the same.
The normal and semicircle laws play parallel roles: classical independent sums retain all pairings in their limiting moments, while free sums retain the noncrossing pairings.

Three ways to use exactly the same eigenvalues
