title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Sampling a Haar unitary correctly
text:
Sampling a Haar unitary correctly
Start with a complex Gaussian matrix \(Z\) and compute a QR decomposition. Correct the phases on the diagonal of \(R\) so that the resulting triangular factor has positive real diagonal. The corresponding unitary factor has Haar distribution. This is the QR construction described by Mezzadri.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

def haar_unitary(n):
    z = (rng.normal(size=(n, n))
         + 1j * rng.normal(size=(n, n))) / np.sqrt(2)
    q, r = np.linalg.qr(z)
    d = np.diag(r)
    return q * (d / np.abs(d))[None, :]

n = 384
signs = np.r_[np.ones(n // 2), -np.ones(n // 2)]
a = np.diag(signs)
u = haar_unitary(n)
b = (u * signs) @ u.conj().T
spectrum = np.linalg.eigvalsh(a + b)
The zero-diagonal event has probability zero for an exact Gaussian draw. Column multiplication by signs implements \(UD_n\), and the conjugate transpose is essential for complex matrices.
The phase correction makes this a general Haar sampler. In this particular conjugation experiment, those column phases cancel against the diagonal \(D_n\), but that cancellation would not justify calling an arbitrary uncorrected QR output Haar.

section: Test a mixed moment, not just a histogram
text:
Test a mixed moment, not just a histogram
The one-variable spectrum of \(A+B\) checks one consequence of freeness. We can also check a word that appears directly in the definition: \[
T_n=\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(ABAB).
\] Both \(A=D_n\) and \(B=U_nD_nU_n^*\) are exactly centered. Freeness predicts \(T_n\to0\).
For the aligned and permuted cases, \(A\) and \(B\) commute and square to the identity, so \(ABAB=I\) and \(T_n=1\) exactly. This is a particularly clear distinction.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Large matrices and finite-size errors
text:
Large matrices and finite-size errors
For deterministic bounded Hermitian sequences with convergent marginal laws, the Haar-rotation theorem controls joint normalized-trace moments for each fixed noncommutative polynomial. The uniformly bounded spectra in this example then let us turn moment convergence for the sum into weak convergence of its empirical spectral measure. Speicher, Section 7.
This does not say that a finite pair is exactly free. It also does not, by itself, provide a finite-size error bound, eigenvalue-spacing statistics, or convergence of the largest eigenvalue.
A simple example explains the last distinction. The matrices \(\operatorname{diag}(10,0,\ldots,0)\) have all fixed positive normalized-trace moments tending to zero, but their largest eigenvalue remains ten. A vanishing fraction of outliers can disappear from a limiting spectral measure. Stronger random-matrix results address such questions, but they require stronger conclusions than ordinary moment convergence.

No. Freeness constrains all alternating products of centered polynomials. One spectral histogram tests only a small part of that joint structure.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Aspect ratio and the Marchenko-Pastur law
text:
Aspect ratio and the Marchenko-Pastur law
Take independent standard complex Gaussian entries, with \(\mathbb E X_{ij}=0\) and \(\mathbb E|X_{ij}|^2=1\). Let \(n,m\to\infty\) with \[
\frac nm\longrightarrow\gamma\in(0,\infty).
\] We normalize the spectral measure by \(1/n\), over all \(n\) eigenvalues of \(C\). Its limiting mean is one.
The Marchenko-Pastur theorem identifies the limit. One moment formulation for this Gaussian model is \[
m_k=\sum_{\pi\in NC(k)}\gamma^{k-|\pi|}.
\] This result comes from Gaussian moment expansion and counting the index sums that survive at leading order. We use that random-matrix theorem as input, rather than proving it from the transform identities. Nica and Speicher, Lecture 22 develop Gaussian moment methods and their connection to Wishart matrices.
Comparing with the free moment-cumulant formula gives \[
\kappa_k=\gamma^{k-1},\qquad
R(w)=\frac1{1-\gamma w}.
\] In particular, \(m_1=1\), \(m_2=1+\gamma\), and the limiting spectral variance is \(\gamma\).
Different references use different parameters for the free Poisson or Marchenko-Pastur law. In the free-Poisson convention with rate \(\lambda\) and jump size \(c\), cumulants are \(\lambda c^k\). Our convention has \(\lambda=1/\gamma\) and \(c=\gamma\).

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: The density and the atom at zero
text:
The density and the atom at zero
Insert the R-transform into the Cauchy-transform equation: \[
z=\frac1G+\frac1{1-\gamma G}.
\] After rearranging, \[
\gamma zG^2-(z+\gamma-1)G+1=0.
\] Let \[
a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2.
\] The branch satisfying \(G(z)\sim1/z\) is \[
G(z)=\frac{z+\gamma-1-\sqrt{(z-a)(z-b)}}{2\gamma z},
\] where the square root is asymptotic to \(z\) at infinity. Stieltjes inversion gives the law \[
\boxed{
\mu_\gamma=
\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0
+\frac{\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}}{2\pi\gamma x}
\mathbf1_{(a,b)}(x)\,dx.
}
\] Here \((r)_+=\max(r,0)\). The continuous density has mass \(\min(1,1/\gamma)\), with the rest at zero.
The atom is also visible before taking a limit. When \(n>m\), a Gaussian \(n\times m\) matrix has rank \(m\) almost surely. Thus \(C\) has exactly \(n-m\) zero eigenvalues, a fraction approaching \(1-1/\gamma\). Keeping only the nonzero eigenvalues and renormalizing them would produce a different probability measure.



Sample covariance spectra for aspect ratios one half, one, and two, with the predicted continuous densities. The final panel has an additional zero atom of mass one half.


Each panel uses one matrix with \(n=320\). In the final panel, the zero eigenvalues are omitted from the density bars, but their probability mass is retained in the normalization and annotated separately.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Find the S-transform without another integral
text:
Find the S-transform without another integral
Let \(w=\psi(t)\) and \(M(t)=1+w\). The moment-cumulant equation from Part III gives \[
w=t(1+w)R(t(1+w))
=\frac{t(1+w)}{1-\gamma t(1+w)}.
\] Solve for \(t\): \[
\chi(w)=\frac{w}{(1+w)(1+\gamma w)}.
\] Consequently, \[
\boxed{S_{\mu_\gamma}(w)=\frac1{1+\gamma w}.}
\] For two free covariance laws with aspect ratios \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\), multiplication gives \[
S(w)=\frac1{(1+\gamma_1w)(1+\gamma_2w)}.
\] The first derivative at zero confirms that the mean-one product has variance \(\gamma_1+\gamma_2\).

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Multiplying square covariance matrices
text:
Multiplying square covariance matrices
Set \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=1\). Consider independent square Gaussian covariance matrices \(A_n,B_n\), each normalized by \(1/n\), and the positive product \[
P_n=A_n^{1/2}B_nA_n^{1/2}.
\] These independent Gaussian covariance ensembles are unitarily invariant and asymptotically free. Their norm control and marginal convergence justify using the positive product law. The limiting S-transform is \[
S(w)=\frac1{(1+w)^2}.
\] With \(t=\chi(w)\), this gives the exceptionally simple equation \[
\boxed{w=t(1+w)^3.}
\] Because \(w=\sum_{k\geq1}m_kt^k\), its coefficients are the desired moments. The first terms follow by substitution: \[
w=t+3t^2+12t^3+55t^4+\cdots.
\] For all orders, the Lagrange inversion identity for \(w=t\phi(w)\) states \[
[t^k]w=\frac1k[u^{k-1}]\phi(u)^k.
\] Using \(\phi(u)=(1+u)^3\) yields \[
m_k=\frac1k\binom{3k}{k-1}
=\boxed{\frac1{2k+1}\binom{3k}{k}}.
\] These are the order-two Fuss-Catalan numbers. The terminology is useful, but the equation \(w=t(1+w)^3\) already gives a direct way to compute them.
The same equation locates the positive right edge. With \(t=1/z\), \[
z=\frac{(1+w)^3}{w}.
\] Starting at large positive \(z\), the physical solution has small positive \(w\). Its first positive turning point satisfies \[
\frac{d}{dw}\frac{(1+w)^3}{w}
=\frac{(1+w)^2(2w-1)}{w^2}=0.
\] Thus \(w=1/2\) and the right endpoint is \(z=27/4\). The resulting law has support \([0,27/4]\). A detailed analysis of this branch and its density appears in Młotkowski, Nowak, Penson, and Życzkowski, Section IV.2.1.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Assumptions to check on a new problem
text:
Assumptions to check on a new problem
The calculations depend on more than knowing the marginal eigenvalue histograms. First specify the normalized matrix and the aspect ratio. Then justify the joint asymptotic-freeness statement. For a product, choose the positive representative and check that the mean permits the ordinary S-transform. Finally, retain the correct Cauchy-transform branch and any atoms when recovering the law.
These checks prevent several tempting mistakes: multiplying eigenvalues coordinate by coordinate, discarding zero eigenvalues, or choosing a convenient root of an algebraic equation without checking its asymptotics.
The series began with the observation that individual eigenvalues leave out relative geometry. Freeness supplies one precise limiting description of that geometry. Cumulants, the R-transform, and the S-transform then turn it into calculations we can test.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: One effective matrix, two parameter blocks
text:
One effective matrix, two parameter blocks
Write a layer as
\[
y=A z,\qquad A=gW,
\]
where \(z\) is fixed for this local calculation and \(g\) is a scalar multiplier. If \(W\) is constrained to Frobenius radius \(R\), then
\[
\lVert A\rVert_F=|g|R.
\]
Fixing \(W\)’s radius has not fixed the forward amplitude when \(g\) remains learnable. For any nonzero target matrix \(A\), choose \(g=\lVert A\rVert_F/R\) and \(W=A/g\). Every such target still has a representative.
This is a single-matrix representation argument. It does not establish that a shared gain can absorb independently chosen scales for many matrices.
With row and column multipliers, the effective map is
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(r)W\operatorname{diag}(c).
\]
These scales can change the distribution of amplification across output and input channels. They are not just another name for one global radius.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Follow the differential through the multiplier
text:
Follow the differential through the multiplier
Let \(G=\partial L/\partial A\) in the usual matrix pairing. For the scalar form \(A=gW\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=gG,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial g}=\langle G,W\rangle_F.
\]
The effective differential is
\[
\delta A=g\,\delta W+W\,\delta g.
\]
Controlling the matrix update alone therefore does not control the whole forward perturbation if the multiplier or its update can grow without bound.
For a normalization gain vector, the corresponding formula is
\[
A=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma),
\qquad
\delta A=\delta W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)
+W\operatorname{diag}(\delta\gamma).
\]
In operator norm this implies
\[
\lVert\delta A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\lVert\gamma\rVert_\infty\lVert\delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
+\lVert W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\delta\gamma\rVert_\infty.
\]
A modular ruler for the effective map needs to account for both contributions. Bounds on matrix motion and bounds on represented-function motion become different when a gain moves too.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Equivalent representations can still learn differently
text:
Equivalent representations can still learn differently
If both factors are free, the transformation \(W\mapsto cW\), \(g\mapsto g/c\) preserves \(A\) for \(c>0\). It can also change ordinary coordinate-based training.
For scalar weights, take \(L(w,g)=(wg)^2/2\). The pairs \((1,1)\) and \((2,1/2)\) represent the same product, one. Use raw SGD with learning rate \(0.1\) for both coordinates.
At \((1,1)\), both gradients equal one. The next pair is \((0.9,0.9)\), with effective product \(0.81\).
At \((2,1/2)\), the gradients are \(1/2\) and two. The next pair is \((1.95,0.3)\), with product \(0.585\).
Both runs began with the same represented function. Their coordinate scales changed the effective update. To first order, separate learning rates give
\[
\delta A=-\eta_W g^2G-\eta_g\langle G,W\rangle_FW.
\]
The finite scalar calculation also includes the product of the two parameter increments. The example is another instance of Part 1’s distinction between a function and the optimizer coordinates used to move it.



Along a function-preserving scalar rescaling, the matrix factor increases and the gain decreases while their product remains fixed. The two equivalent starting pairs in the worked example nevertheless produce different effective products after one coordinate SGD step.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: A shared gain cannot make every branch independent
text:
A shared gain cannot make every branch independent
Suppose two branches use
\[
A_1=W_1\operatorname{diag}(\gamma),
\qquad A_2=W_2\operatorname{diag}(\gamma).
\]
A common rescaling of both matrices can be absorbed by the gain. Rescaling just one matrix and changing the shared gain to compensate also changes the other branch.
Independent branch multipliers \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) can restore a relative-amplitude freedom that a single shared scalar does not provide. Whether those amplitudes matter depends on where the branches meet. Addition makes relative branch strength visible. A product introduces a different compensation symmetry.
For example, scalar query and key multipliers appear in attention scores through their product. Changing one up and the other down can preserve those scores. Scaling both in the same direction generally changes the score scale before softmax. A value multiplier can also interact with the output projection instead of controlling an independent final amplitude.
The architecture determines the redundant directions. A list of tensor norms does not determine them by itself.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Learnable scales do not remove the need for scale management
text:
Learnable scales do not remove the need for scale management
Learnable Multipliers studies scalar and row/column forward multipliers while leaving the underlying matrices subject to decay. Its Section 4.1 discusses redundant parameter symmetries and the numerical drift they can permit. The authors use light decay on multipliers to control that drift in their experiments.
The general distinction matters more than copying a decay coefficient. A scale can be useful for the forward function, redundant in a joint parameterization, or involved in both a useful relative scale and an unstable coordinate direction.
Positive log-parameterizations can make multiplicative changes easy to express, but they change the optimizer coordinates and exclude negative gains unless signs are handled separately. Removing a redundant factor can improve identifiability, but removing an independent branch multiplier may remove a useful degree of freedom.
These are different interventions. They should be compared through the effective map, not only through whether the parameter norms look tidy.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: A joint effective ruler has a kernel
text:
A joint effective ruler has a kernel
There is a natural temptation to measure the tuple \((\delta W,\delta\gamma)\) by the size of \(\delta A\). That does measure the represented linear-map change. But it is generally a seminorm on the redundant parameters.
For example, the infinitesimal transformation
\[
\delta W=tW,\qquad\delta\gamma=-t\gamma
\]
has nonzero parameter motion and zero effective differential. A genuine norm cannot vanish on that nonzero direction.
One can remove the redundancy by a coordinate convention, or work with equivalence classes of parameters that represent the same function. Calling a pulled-back measurement a norm without addressing its kernel skips a mathematical step.
The practical question is whether such a joint construction makes an affordable optimizer with a useful consequence. The existence of a symmetry alone does not establish that result.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Which quantities should remain available?
text:
Which quantities should remain available?
Before fixing a forward scale, identify the function it controls, every consumer that shares it, and the transformations that can compensate it. Then ask whether the complete collection of constraints still admits the intended functions.
This gives us a more precise goal than either freeing every multiplier or fixing every tensor norm. Control redundant coordinate drift while preserving useful relative scales. The next post turns that goal into an exact compatibility calculation for several matrices sharing one gain.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Try tracking the effective map
text:
Try tracking the effective map

In the scalar SGD example, verify the effective products \(0.81\) and \(0.585\) after one step.
Show directly that the infinitesimal common rescaling of \(W\) and \(\gamma\) has zero \(\delta A\).



Answer sketches


Choose \(g=3/2\) and \(W=2A/3\). Then \(gW=A\) and \(\lVert W\rVert_F=2\).
The gradients of \((wg)^2/2\) are \(g(wg)\) and \(w(wg)\). Substitute each starting pair, apply the two coordinate updates, and multiply the new factors.
Substitute into the differential: \(tW\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)-tW\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)=0\).

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: First reproduce the claim in a setting it actually covers
text:
First reproduce the claim in a setting it actually covers
Use fixed isotropic features and two target maps whose Frobenius norms are one and \(b>0\). Impose individual radii \(R_1=R_2=1\) and a shared scalar gain. Part 11 gives
\[
g_*=(1+b)/2,\qquad
\mathcal L_*=(b-1)^2/4.
\]
This is a prediction over a whole family of target imbalances, rather than a single failed training curve.
For a small reproducible check, I used four-dimensional features taking the eight values \(z=\pm2e_j\) with equal weight. Their second moment is exactly \(I\). A fixed matrix \(A_1\) has Frobenius norm one, and \(A_2=bA_1\). The code evaluates the actual branch-output squared loss at the constrained optimum.
Across 45 ratios from \(0.25\) to three, this evaluated loss matches the formula within \(10^{-12}\). A joint group radius and independent branch multipliers both give zero fitting loss to numerical precision in the same calculation.



The minimum branch-fitting loss rises quadratically as the target norm ratio moves away from one under individual radii and a shared scalar gain. A joint radius and independent branch multipliers preserve the prescribed target maps and give zero loss in the same frozen-feature experiment.


These are direct finite-design evaluations, not neural-network training results. They check the algebra and the proposed intervention’s feasible set. Optimizer convergence is a separate experiment.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Attention can preserve products while changing branches
text:
Attention can preserve products while changing branches
For a bias-free attention head, using column-vector inputs, write
\[
q=W_Qx,\quad k=W_Kx',\quad v=W_Vx.
\]
Without positional rotations, the score depends on \(W_Q^\top W_K\). The value-output composition depends on \(W_OW_V\). For invertible matrices \(S\) and \(T\) of the appropriate head dimensions, the transformations
\[
W_Q\mapsto SW_Q,\qquad W_K\mapsto S^{-\top}W_K
\]
and
\[
W_V\mapsto TW_V,\qquad W_O\mapsto W_OT^{-1}
\]
preserve those products. The individual branch maps and their Frobenius norms may change.
Thus failure to preserve each \(W_i\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)\) is not enough to establish failure to preserve the attention function. Even equality of score matrices is sufficient rather than necessary for equality of softmax weights, since rowwise additive constants cancel.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: An explicit escape from the branch obstruction
text:
An explicit escape from the branch obstruction
Consider a scalar head with no positional rotations. The unconstrained teacher uses the shared gain \(g=1\) and
\[
W_Q=1,\quad W_K=2,\quad W_V=1,\quad W_O=1.
\]
Its query, key, and value maps are respectively \(x\), \(2x\), and \(x\). Part 11’s shared-gain reasoning rules out preserving all three maps while setting \(|W_Q|=|W_K|=|W_V|=1\).
Now require those three unit radii but leave \(W_O\) unconstrained. Choose
\[
g'=\sqrt2,\quad W_Q'=W_K'=W_V'=1,
\quad W_O'=1/\sqrt2.
\]
The new query and key maps are both \(\sqrt2x\). Their product is still \(2xx'\), so the softmax attention weights are unchanged for every input sequence. The values scale by \(\sqrt2\), which the output projection cancels. The final attention output is identical.
The code verifies this directly on a small token sequence. More importantly, the displayed product identities prove it for arbitrary scalar token inputs in this specified architecture.
This is a negative control with teeth. The branch-map obstruction is real, yet it does not imply an output-function obstruction under these constraints. Fixing the output projection too would be a different question and would require another analysis.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Positional operations restrict the available transformations
text:
Positional operations restrict the available transformations
With rotary position matrices \(R_p\), a query-key score contains
\[
x^\top W_Q^\top R_p^\top R_q W_Kx'.
\]
After the general factor transformation above, the middle expression becomes
\[
W_Q^\top S^\top R_p^\top R_q S^{-\top}W_K.
\]
An arbitrary \(S\) no longer cancels. Scalar rebalancing \(S=cI\) still does. Other surviving transformations depend on the positional operators and the rest of the architecture.
Query/key normalization, shared heads, biases, masks, and nonlinear gates can alter the analysis again. The correct equivalence class belongs to the actual computation graph, not to a convenient isolated matrix identity.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Measure the mechanism before running a leaderboard
text:
Measure the mechanism before running a leaderboard
A useful progression has several stages.

Frozen branch teachers. Vary target imbalance and gain bounds. Compare measured fitting losses with the exact floor and channelwise feasibility criterion.
Frozen attention teachers. Supervise score and final-output behavior. Optimize over the remaining factorization freedoms before declaring a capacity restriction. Include the scalar escape above as a control the analysis must get right.
Learned features. Let upstream representations adapt. Determine whether they remove the predicted restriction or merely hide it behind extreme gain conditioning.
Completed training comparisons. Only after a mechanism survives the earlier tests, compare tuned decay, fixed norms, grouped constraints, and existing multiplier baselines at matched data and tuning budgets.

The observable should follow the claim. A branch reconstruction error measures a different target from final task loss. Parameter norms, angular displacement, effective map changes, and gain trajectories diagnose different parts of the mechanism.
When intervening at a checkpoint, preserve the represented function and transport optimizer state according to the convention being tested. Resetting moments changes the intervention. If an exact state transport is unavailable, measure and report that limitation.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: What would strengthen or weaken the direction?
text:
What would strengthen or weaken the direction?
The explanation strengthens if compatibility or bounded-gain conditioning predicts a failure on new targets, survives the correct attention symmetries, and predicts a repair that transfers to learned-feature tasks. An effect that survives angular-schedule controls is more informative than an early curve at one nominal learning rate.
It weakens if alternative factorizations remove the restriction, upstream features absorb it, or existing multipliers and scheduling explain all practically relevant differences. Those outcomes should change the research direction rather than be relabeled as optimizer improvements.
The mathematical burden also includes prior work. A positive-feasibility criterion is an elementary matrix-scaling calculation. A publishable novelty claim needs a broader comparison with existing scaling, invariant optimization, and normalization results, not just an unfamiliar notation.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Return to the question about scale
text:
Return to the question about scale
The series began with identical predictors taking different gradient steps. That forced us to distinguish functions from coordinates. Weight decay, momentum, layer norms, support directions, and manifold constraints each exposed another part of that distinction.
The final question is sharper than fixing all norms or freeing all gains: which redundant scales can be controlled while preserving useful module behavior, and what measurable consequence follows?
We have exact toy calculations and controls that can reject an overly broad interpretation. We do not yet have evidence of a new optimizer advantage on a trainable Transformer. That is the research program to carry beyond these twelve posts.

Verify the query-key and value-output products in the scalar attention escape.

The original query-key product is \(1\times2=2\), and the new one is \(\sqrt2\times\sqrt2=2\). The value-output product is one in both cases.
Its own branch maps are feasible by construction. Use prescribed teachers, unconstrained target maps, or alternative representatives that test a prediction beyond that tautology.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Fix the convention before interpreting the penalty
text:
Fix the convention before interpreting the penalty
Let \(L_t\) be the data loss on the minibatch used at step \(t\). Assume a positive rescaling of the block \(w\) preserves the model’s predictions, so that
\[
L_t(cw)=L_t(w),\qquad c>0.
\]
All other parameters are fixed in this calculation. The identity must hold for every minibatch used, and we stay away from \(w=0\).
Our update is raw SGD without momentum:
\[
w_{t+1}=a_t w_t-\eta_t\nabla L_t(w_t),
\qquad a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t>0.
\]
Take \(\eta_t>0\) and \(\lambda_t\geq0\). For this algorithm, adding the penalty \(\lambda_t\|w\|_2^2/2\) to the current loss produces exactly the displayed update. With an adaptive preconditioner or a momentum buffer, we must inspect the actual equations before making that identification.
For the data loss, all radii on a positive ray are equivalent. Along that ray, the penalty can be made arbitrarily small by shrinking \(w\). It therefore does not directly distinguish a simpler predictor from a more complicated one within this equivalence class. That does not make the training dynamics, or their eventual effect on generalization, irrelevant.
This distinction is the starting point of van Laarhoven’s normalization analysis, Sections 2 through 4. It concerns a specified symmetry, not every weight in a normalized network.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: The radius records what decay and gradients do together
text:
The radius records what decay and gradients do together
Write \(w_t=R_t e_t\) with \(R_t>0\) and \(\|e_t\|_2=1\). Define \(h_t=\nabla L_t(e_t)\). The scale identities from Part 1 give
\[
\nabla L_t(w_t)=\frac{h_t}{R_t},
\qquad \langle e_t,h_t\rangle=0.
\]
The radial and tangent parts of the update are perpendicular. Squaring its norm gives the exact recurrence
\[
R_{t+1}^2
=a_t^2R_t^2+\frac{\eta_t^2}{R_t^2}\|h_t\|_2^2.
\]
Decay contributes the first term. The finite gradient displacement contributes the second. A tangent step can increase a radius even though its first-order radial derivative is zero.
The corresponding direction is
\[
e_{t+1}
=\frac{e_t-\alpha_t h_t}{\|e_t-\alpha_t h_t\|_2},
\qquad
\alpha_t=\frac{\eta_t}{a_tR_t^2}.
\]
Here \(\alpha_t\) is the coefficient in the exact normalized update. The actual rotation obeys \(\tan\theta_t=\alpha_t\|h_t\|_2\). An effective learning rate, a displacement length, and an angle are related quantities, but they are not interchangeable.
At the same current weight and gradient, decreasing \(a_t\) increases the rotation. Across different training runs, however, the weights and gradients soon differ. This one-step comparison is not a theorem that stronger decay always helps or always produces faster progress.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Replace decay with a different learning-rate schedule
text:
Replace decay with a different learning-rate schedule
There is a stronger statement than the local observation about \(R_t\).
Define the cumulative shrinkage
\[
c_0=1,\qquad c_{t+1}=a_t c_t,
\]
and introduce coordinates \(z_t=w_t/c_t\). Since every \(c_t\) is positive, \(z_t\) and \(w_t\) represent the same predictor. Their gradients satisfy
\[
\nabla L_t(w_t)=\frac1{c_t}\nabla L_t(z_t).
\]
Substitute \(w_t=c_tz_t\) into the SGD update and divide by \(c_{t+1}\):
\[
z_{t+1}
=z_t-\widetilde\eta_t\nabla L_t(z_t),
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=\frac{\eta_t}{c_t c_{t+1}}.
\]
There is no decay in the \(z\) update. Its learning rate has changed instead. Starting both runs from the same weight, using the same minibatches, and using this transformed schedule makes their predictions agree at every step, under the stated symmetry.
No equilibrium, averaging, or small-step approximation entered this derivation. If the minibatches are random, it is an identity for the same realized sequence of minibatches. The exact prediction agreement also uses the assumed forward symmetry, rather than merely an equality of scalar losses.
For constant \(\eta\) and \(a=1-\eta\lambda\), the formula simplifies to
\[
c_t=a^t,\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=\eta a^{-(2t+1)}.
\]
The first transformed learning rate is \(\eta/a\). Each subsequent one is larger by the factor \(a^{-2}\). This is the momentum-free equivalence studied in Li and Arora’s Section 2.1. The initialization and first-step factor matter.
The word clock is shorthand for this change in step coefficients. It does not mean that an arbitrary finite-step training run is the same trajectory played back faster.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: One toy run in two coordinate systems
text:
One toy run in two coordinate systems
Return to our predictor \(f_w(x)=w^\top x/\|w\|_2\), input \(x=(0,1)\), and target \(1\):
\[
L(w)=\frac12\left(\frac{w_2}{\|w\|_2}-1\right)^2.
\]
Use \(w_0=(1,0)\), \(\eta=0.1\), and \(\lambda=1\), so \(a=0.9\). These deliberately simple numbers illustrate the identity, not a recommended training configuration.
The decayed first step is \(w_1=(0.9,0.1)\). The matched run has no decay and starts with learning rate \(0.1/0.9\), giving \(z_1=(1,1/9)\). Since \(w_1=0.9z_1\), their predictions agree exactly. Both rotate by approximately \(6.34^\circ\).
The first three transformed learning rates are approximately \(0.111111\), \(0.137174\), and \(0.169351\). Keeping the no-decay learning rate fixed at \(0.1\) would not give the same run.



A 24-step toy calculation. Decayed SGD shrinks the weight radius while the equivalent no-decay coordinates keep a radius close to one. Their prediction curves overlap.


The figure computes both recurrences independently. Their prediction discrepancy stays below \(10^{-12}\) in this calculation. This verifies the example numerically. The algebra above is what establishes the equivalence.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: An equilibrium estimate needs one more assumption
text:
An equilibrium estimate needs one more assumption
The radius recurrence is exact, but \(\|h_t\|_2^2\) changes with direction and minibatch. To get a simple scalar model, freeze that quantity at a positive constant \(Q\), and also hold \(\eta>0\) and \(\lambda>0\) fixed with \(0<a<1\).
If this simplified recurrence has a fixed radius \(R_*\), then
\[
R_*^4=\frac{\eta^2Q}{1-a^2}
\approx\frac{\eta Q}{2\lambda},
\qquad \eta\lambda\ll1.
\]
The approximation uses \(1-(1-\eta\lambda)^2\approx2\eta\lambda\). It does not follow from scale invariance alone. In our deterministic toy problem, the directional gradient becomes small as the prediction approaches its target, so holding \(Q\) fixed would miss part of the dynamics.
For stochastic gradients, replacing \(Q\) by an average also requires care: the radius and gradient magnitude may be correlated, and an expectation of an inverse radius is not the inverse of an expected radius. A stationary-radius heuristic is not the same result as the pathwise schedule identity.
This is where the distinctions in the Intrinsic Learning Rate paper become useful. Its direction-and-radius SDE and its Fast Equilibrium Conjecture have their own assumptions. Neither licenses a universal statement that every optimizer on every architecture depends only on \(\eta\lambda\).

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: What a decay comparison must hold fixed
text:
What a decay comparison must hold fixed
On a truly invariant block, decay can change the optimization path without directly changing the predictor when applied alone. Those are compatible facts.
To understand a comparison, I want the actual shrinkage factor \(a_t\), the nominal learning rate, the radius, and the angular displacement. Matching only the nominal learning rate can leave the directional dynamics unmatched. Matching one angle still does not establish matching useful feature changes.
We also cannot transfer the derivation unchanged to epsilon-sensitive normalization, scale-sensitive gains, or a block that is only invariant under a joint transformation with another parameter. Part 2 explains why those distinctions matter.
Next comes a complication that is present even under perfect forward invariance: the optimizer remembers. The current gradient is tangent, but its memory need not be.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Try changing the clock
text:
Try changing the clock

Set \(\lambda=0\). What happens to \(c_t\) and the transformed schedule?
With constant \(a=0.9\), what is the ratio \(\widetilde\eta_{t+1}/\widetilde\eta_t\)? Why is it not \(1/a\)?
In the frozen-\(Q\) model, take \(\eta=0.1\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(Q=1\). Compute the exact fixed radius and its angular step.



Answer sketches


Every \(a_t=1\), so \(c_t=1\) and \(\widetilde\eta_t=\eta_t\). The change of coordinates becomes the identity.
The ratio is \(1/0.9^2\approx1.234568\). Both \(c_t\) and \(c_{t+1}\) appear in the denominator of the transformed learning rate.
\(R_*=(0.01/0.19)^{1/4}\approx0.4790\). At that fixed point, \(\tan\theta=\sqrt{1-a^2}/a\), so \(\cos\theta=a\) and \(\theta\approx25.84^\circ\). These are predictions of the frozen-\(Q\) model, not of the earlier fitting trajectory.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Hold the input fixed and look at the output
text:
Hold the input fixed and look at the output
Let \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(y=Wx\). Change the weights by a matrix \(\Delta W\), keeping the input fixed. The activation change is
\[
\Delta y=(W+\Delta W)x-Wx=\Delta W x.
\]
This is exact. There is no neglected higher-order term because the layer is linear in \(W\) at a fixed \(x\).
Suppose we measure input and output size with norms \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_X\) and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_Y\). The induced operator norm is
\[
N_{X\to Y}(\Delta W)
=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_Y}{\lVert x\rVert_X}.
\]
It gives the bound
\[
\lVert\Delta y\rVert_Y
\leq N_{X\to Y}(\Delta W)\lVert x\rVert_X.
\]
If inputs have norm at most one, the matrix norm is a worst-case activation-change budget. The choices of input and output norms specify what that promise means.
This is the starting point of Bernstein and Newhouse’s treatment of layer geometry, especially Sections 3.3 and 4.1. The semantics of the layer determine which operator norm is worth considering.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Equal Frobenius size can hide different worst cases
text:
Equal Frobenius size can hide different worst cases
With Euclidean norms on both activation spaces, the induced norm is the spectral norm:
\[
N_{2\to2}(\Delta W)=\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
=\sigma_{\max}(\Delta W).
\]
Compare two perturbations in two dimensions:
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have Frobenius norm one. But \(A\) can move the output by one on a unit input, while \(B\) moves every unit input by \(1/\sqrt2\). Thus
\[
\lVert A\rVert_F=\lVert B\rVert_F=1,
\qquad
\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=1,
\qquad
\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=1/\sqrt2.
\]



Images of the Euclidean unit input circle under two perturbations with Frobenius norm one. A maps the circle to a line segment reaching radius one. B maps it to a circle of radius one over square root two.


The distinction grows with width. In \(n\) dimensions, a rank-one matrix with its only nonzero singular value equal to one has the same Frobenius norm as \(I/\sqrt n\). Their operator norms are one and \(1/\sqrt n\).
Frobenius size adds energy across singular directions. Spectral size asks for the largest response in any one direction. Neither description is meaningless. They answer different questions.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: An average asks a different question again
text:
An average asks a different question again
Suppose \(x\) is uniformly distributed on the Euclidean unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^n\). Then \(\mathbb E[xx^\top]=I/n\), and
\[
\mathbb E\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_2^2
=\frac1n\operatorname{tr}(\Delta W^\top\Delta W)
=\frac1n\lVert\Delta W\rVert_F^2.
\]
For our two-dimensional \(A\) and \(B\), this mean squared activation change is \(1/2\) in both cases. Their worst cases differ, but this particular average agrees.
More generally, if \(C=\mathbb E[xx^\top]\) is the input second-moment matrix,
\[
\mathbb E\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_2^2
=\operatorname{tr}(\Delta W C\Delta W^\top).
\]
This formula uses the second moment, not necessarily the covariance. They agree when the input mean is zero.
A weight perturbation can be large on a direction the data rarely uses. Conversely, a modest-looking change can align with a frequently amplified feature. The uniform-sphere calculation does not establish what is typical under an arbitrary training distribution.
Before debating which matrix norm is best, decide whether the goal is a worst-case guarantee, a distributional average, or another functional quantity. The matrix entries alone do not make that choice for us.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: RMS measurements introduce an explicit width factor
text:
RMS measurements introduce an explicit width factor
For a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\frac{\lVert x\rVert_2}{\sqrt n}.
\]
This measures a typical coordinate scale. A vector with all coordinates equal to one has RMS norm one at every width, while its Euclidean norm grows as \(\sqrt n\).
Use RMS norms on the input and output of \(y=Wx\). Substituting their definitions into the operator norm gives
\[
N_{\mathrm{RMS}\to\mathrm{RMS}}(\Delta W)
=\sqrt{\frac n m}\,\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
The factor is \(\sqrt{n/m}\), with input width in the numerator. A budget \(N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon\) therefore allows
\[
\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\epsilon\sqrt{\frac m n}.
\]
For a map from four inputs to sixteen outputs, a perturbation with spectral norm one has RMS-to-RMS norm \(1/2\). For a map from sixteen inputs to four outputs, the same spectral norm corresponds to RMS-to-RMS norm two. The worst-case RMS responses differ by a factor of four.
These are choices of measurement for the same forward expression \(y=Wx\). RMS is a ruler here, not an extra RMSNorm operation inserted into the network. Conventions that rescale the forward function itself can move width factors elsewhere, so the forward equation and the norm must be read together.
This width factor will reappear in the next post’s update direction. It comes from the activation geometry before we choose an optimizer.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: A lookup table has different input semantics
text:
A lookup table has different input semantics
A dense layer may receive mixtures of input coordinates. An embedding lookup receives a one-hot vector \(e_j\), and its output is simply column \(j\) of the embedding matrix \(E\).
If we want every lookup to have a bounded Euclidean output change, the relevant quantity is
\[
\max_j\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2.
\]
This is also the induced \(\ell_1\)-to-Euclidean norm. Indeed,
\[
\lVert\Delta E x\rVert_2
\leq\sum_j |x_j|\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2
\leq\lVert x\rVert_1\max_j\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2.
\]
Equality is attained by choosing a one-hot input for a largest column. With an RMS output ruler, divide the column lengths by \(\sqrt m\).
The same matrix can look different under the dense-layer question. Take
\[
\Delta E=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each lookup changes the Euclidean output by one. But the Euclidean unit input \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) combines the columns and produces an output of length \(\sqrt2\). The spectral norm sees that mixture, while the lookup budget need not.
The distinction is what the input can be. Matrix shape does not tell us whether the module is a dense transformation or a categorical lookup. Bernstein and Newhouse make this explicit in their Linear and Embed examples in Section 4.1.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Let the input move and a second term appears
text:
Let the input move and a second term appears
So far, we have held \(x\) fixed. If upstream parameters also change the input by \(\Delta x\), then
\[
(W+\Delta W)(x+\Delta x)-Wx
=\Delta W x+W\Delta x+\Delta W\Delta x.
\]
The first two terms form the differential. The final term is a finite-step interaction. For Euclidean measurements, for example,
\[
\lVert\Delta y\rVert_2
\leq\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert x\rVert_2
+\lVert W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\Delta x\rVert_2
+\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\Delta x\rVert_2.
\]
A local weight-update budget controls the first contribution. It does not erase input sensitivity or the interaction term. Shared normalization gains from Part 2 also belong in the joint perturbation when they move.
This is why a layerwise measurement is a starting point for network geometry. Composing modules requires accounting for how one module’s output perturbation becomes another’s input perturbation. We will reach that question in Part 7.
For now, the layer’s role gives us a constraint set for its update. The next question is how to choose a direction within that set to reduce the loss.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Try changing the ruler
text:
Try changing the ruler

In four dimensions, compare the Frobenius and operator norms of \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0,0)\) and \(B=I/2\). What is their common mean squared response on uniformly distributed unit inputs?
For a layer with nine input and four output coordinates, what spectral update budget gives an RMS-to-RMS budget of \(0.1\)?
For the two-column lookup example above, compare the largest column’s RMS change with the RMS-to-RMS operator norm of the same matrix.



Answer sketches


Both Frobenius norms are one. The operator norms are one and \(1/2\). The common mean squared response is \(1/4\).
\(\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq0.1\sqrt{4/9}=1/15\approx0.066667\).
The largest column RMS is \(1/\sqrt2\). Since input and output dimensions are both two, the RMS-to-RMS norm equals the spectral norm, \(\sqrt2\). Their input unit sets differ, so this is not a contradiction.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Begin with a bound on the computation
text:
Begin with a bound on the computation
Suppose local perturbation analysis gives
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq\sum_{i=1}^k c_i N_i(\delta W_i),
\]
where \(N_i\) measures a module’s weight perturbation and each \(c_i>0\) accounts for its downstream sensitivity. This is a bound on the differential at the point under discussion. A finite-step bound needs the corresponding remainder control.
For a composition \(f_2\circ f_1\), for example, a sensitivity bound \(s_2\) for the second module leads to contributions of the form
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq s_2N_1(\delta W_1)+N_2(\delta W_2),
\]
assuming the module norms and input domain make those local bounds valid. The earlier module pays for amplification through the later one.
We now want a single norm on the whole update tuple. Choose positive masses \(m_i\) summing to one, and set
\[
N_{\max}(\delta W)=\max_i\frac{c_iN_i(\delta W_i)}{m_i}.
\]
If \(N_{\max}(\delta W)\leq\epsilon\), then \(c_iN_i(\delta W_i)\leq m_i\epsilon\) for each module. Adding these inequalities proves
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq\epsilon.
\]
Mass is a share of this bound. It is not a claim that each layer will learn equally useful features, or that the assigned share is always fully used by the true output change.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: The maximum creates a product of local balls
text:
The maximum creates a product of local balls
The global unit ball is exactly
\[
\{\delta W:N_{\max}(\delta W)\leq1\}
=\prod_i\{\delta W_i:N_i(\delta W_i)\leq m_i/c_i\}.
\]
The constraints are independent once their radii are chosen. One layer does not consume another’s radius simply by taking a nonzero step. That product structure is the key geometric property.
Let \(G_i\) be the loss differential for block \(i\), represented through its usual coordinate pairing. Maximizing the global linear functional separates into one support problem per block:
\[
N_{\max}^*(G)=\sum_i\frac{m_i}{c_i}N_i^*(G_i).
\]
If \(D_i\) is a unit-ball support maximizer for \(G_i\), one globally steepest fixed-radius descent update is
\[
\delta W_i=-\epsilon\frac{m_i}{c_i}D_i.
\]
Every block with nonzero gradient can saturate its assigned local radius at once. Zero gradients and ties permit nonunique choices. Choosing zero on an inactive block is convenient.
This is parallel budget use, not a guarantee that all blocks make comparable progress. Sensitivity and gradient geometry still differ.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: A two-module calculation
text:
A two-module calculation
Take two scalar blocks with \(c=(2,1)\), masses \(m=(1/4,3/4)\), and gradient coordinates \(G=(6,1)\). The global norm is
\[
N_{\max}(d)=\max(8|d_1|,\,4|d_2|/3).
\]
The positive support maximizer is \(d=(1/8,3/4)\). It has
\[
G^\top d=6/8+3/4=3/2,
\qquad 2|d_1|+|d_2|=1.
\]
The actual descent update is \(-\epsilon d\). The first block receives a smaller parameter displacement because its output effect is amplified by a factor of two and its mass is smaller.
There is no missing global rescaling to divide the remaining budget between these two directions. The maximum already allocated both radii.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: A sum asks the optimizer to make a different allocation
text:
A sum asks the optimizer to make a different allocation
The functional bound also suggests the valid norm
\[
N_{\mathrm{sum}}(d)=\sum_i c_iN_i(d_i).
\]
Its dual norm is
\[
N_{\mathrm{sum}}^*(G)=\max_i\frac{N_i^*(G_i)}{c_i}.
\]
With a unique largest ratio, a support maximizer can spend the entire budget on that block. In our example, the ratios are three and one. The sum-budget maximizer is \((1/2,0)\), with support value three.
A weighted quadratic aggregation gives an intermediate geometry:
\[
N_2(d)=\left[\sum_i m_i
\left(\frac{c_iN_i(d_i)}{m_i}\right)^2\right]^{1/2},
\]
\[
N_2^*(G)=\left[\sum_i m_i
\left(\frac{N_i^*(G_i)}{c_i}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}.
\]
Here its support value is \(\sqrt3\), attained at approximately \((0.216506,0.433013)\). The three norms control the same stated linearized feature bound, but their feasible sets and allocations differ.



Three ways to allocate the two-module budget. A weighted maximum gives a rectangle, a quadratic aggregation an ellipse, and a weighted sum a diamond. Their support maximizers for the same gradient occur at different points.


The larger support value of the sum budget is not an optimization victory over the maximum. Its unit ball is larger here. The question is which allocation describes the changes we want to permit.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: What recursive modular geometry adds
text:
What recursive modular geometry adds
In a network, the coefficients are not a list of independent tuning constants pasted onto unrelated layers. Composition propagates input sensitivity through downstream modules. Concatenation combines outputs under a specified output-space norm. The module tree determines how those rules are applied.
Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm develops this recursive construction. Modular Duality then derives the corresponding support directions. The distinction parallels Part 6: normalizing a proposal in a norm and solving the norm’s support problem are different operations.
Our simple product-ball derivation explains one important property of the weighted maximum. It does not by itself establish all the curvature bounds or learning-rate transfer results of the modular framework. Those require the papers’ module assumptions and composition arguments.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Where the choice still needs judgment
text:
Where the choice still needs judgment
The norm depends on the chosen module boundary. If a gain and several matrices jointly determine an effective map, treating each matrix as an independent atom may leave out part of the perturbation. A different outer aggregation cannot repair that missing dependency.
Masses also encode priorities. They can reserve more possible feature motion for one part of the computation, but a bound on motion is not a bound on its usefulness. Task progress still depends on gradients, data, and nonlinear interactions.
The maximum earns its place because it gives explicit local radii and parallel support problems. It is a design with consequences, not a uniqueness theorem. Changing it is mathematically possible. A useful alternative needs a reason for its different allocation.
Next we add a distinct kind of restriction: the weights themselves may have to remain on a constraint set. That restriction changes which directions are admissible even before we choose their size.

section: Try allocating the budget
text:
Try allocating the budget

In the two-module example, verify that the maximum-budget support direction obeys the unit feature bound.
Keep \(c=(2,1)\) but use equal masses. What local radii and support value does the maximum give for \(G=(6,1)\)?
Why does the sum budget admit an optimizer that changes only the first block in the original example?



Answer sketches


\(2(1/8)+3/4=1\), while the gradient pairing is \(3/2\).
The radii are \(1/4\) and \(1/2\). The support value is \(6/4+1/2=2\).
Its dual compares \(6/2=3\) with \(1/1=1\). The first block offers more linear decrease per unit of that sum budget, so \((1/2,0)\) is a support maximizer.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Write down the wrapper exactly
text:
Write down the wrapper exactly
The Hyperball paper defines a Frobenius normalization \(\operatorname{Normalize}(X)=X/\lVert X\rVert_F\) and a fixed radius \(R>0\). Given a nonzero base proposal \(u_t\) and step parameter \(\eta_t\geq0\), its update is
\[
W_{t+1}=R\operatorname{Normalize}
\left(W_t-\eta_tR\operatorname{Normalize}(u_t)\right).
\]
The matrix starts on the radius-\(R\) sphere. The trial displacement has Frobenius length \(\eta_tR\). The return map restores the weight norm to \(R\).
The final chord \(W_{t+1}-W_t\) need not have length \(\eta_tR\). This difference is visible even before considering what base optimizer produced \(u_t\).
The normalization requires nonzero arguments. A zero proposal needs a defined no-step convention. A zero trial point also needs an implementation guard rather than division by its norm.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Two fixed norms leave one angle unfixed
text:
Two fixed norms leave one angle unfixed
Write \(E=W/R\) and \(U=u/\lVert u\rVert_F\), so both have Frobenius norm one. Let
\[
\rho=\langle E,U\rangle_F,
\qquad U_T=U-\rho E,
\qquad\lVert U_T\rVert_F=\sqrt{1-\rho^2}.
\]
The trial direction is
\[
E-\eta U=(1-\eta\rho)E-\eta U_T.
\]
Radial renormalization preserves that direction. For a nonzero trial point, the actual rotation is therefore
\[
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(\eta\sqrt{1-\rho^2},\,1-\eta\rho\right).
\]
When \(\rho=0\), this reduces to \(\theta=\arctan\eta\). Otherwise, the same value of \(\eta\) can give a different angle. For \(\eta=1/2\), the tangent proposal gives approximately \(26.57^\circ\), while \(\rho=-0.8\) gives approximately \(12.09^\circ\).
The final chord length is
\[
\lVert W_{t+1}-W_t\rVert_F=2R\sin(\theta/2).
\]
If \(U=E\) and \(0<\eta<1\), the trial point shrinks along the radius and renormalization returns exactly to the starting weight. There was a nonzero proposal budget and no final motion.



For a fixed normalized proposal length of one half of the weight radius, the actual rotation varies with the weight-proposal correlation. The tangent case is about 26.57 degrees, while a correlation of minus 0.8 gives about 12.09 degrees.


Fixed norms make the geometry more explicit. They do not make the remaining variable disappear. This is controlled length, not automatically a fixed angular step.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: A one-step schedule match we can derive exactly
text:
A one-step schedule match we can derive exactly
Compare a free-radius update at \(w=R_tE\):
\[
w^+=aR_tE-\alpha U,\qquad a>0.
\]
If the unit proposal \(U\) is the same in both comparisons, choosing
\[
\alpha=aR_t\eta
\]
gives \(w^+=aR_t(E-\eta U)\). The free-radius update and the Hyperball update have exactly the same next direction. Their radii differ.
This equality holds for radial as well as tangent proposals. It is a conditional one-step identity: we assumed the same current direction and the same normalized proposal. Those conditions do not automatically persist when optimizer states, scale-sensitive parameters, or data-dependent proposal directions evolve differently.
Part 3 gave a whole-trajectory equivalence under its own assumptions. Part 4 showed why optimizer memory must also transform. A schedule intervention in a real matrix optimizer should not silently inherit either theorem.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: What the two papers establish
text:
What the two papers establish
Hyperball Optimization studies the fixed-radius wrapper with base optimizers and reports benefits in its pretraining comparisons. Its Section 4 separates an expressivity argument from a model of radius and angular dynamics. The stationary analysis assumes an infinite optimizer history and iid isotropic Gaussian optimizer inputs. Its angular interpretation uses an ansatz, rather than a pathwise theorem for every training run.
Hyperball May Not Be a Free Lunch explicitly includes the parameter-proposal angle and tests schedule interventions. In its tested settings, aligning angular effective steps reproduces a substantial part of the validation-loss behavior. That result motivates a control, not a universal equality of all optimizer trajectories.
The productive question is whether a claimed benefit survives comparisons that account for the induced schedule. Simply giving both methods the same nominal learning rate does not answer it.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Separate the interventions before comparing them
text:
Separate the interventions before comparing them
For a useful experiment, distinguish the base proposal rule, weight-radius constraint, proposal normalization, and external schedule. Changing all four at once makes the source of an improvement ambiguous.
Start with a common base optimizer and a fully specified state initialization. Compare decay and fixed-radius versions under their tuned schedules. Measure the true angle, proposal-weight correlation, radius, effective map change, and final task loss. A matched-angle control is useful even if it does not reproduce every feature of the trajectory.
If one method needs extra matrix operations, report that work. If a correction depends on a reference run’s recorded angles, identify the reference information it uses. An intervention that diagnoses a mechanism is not automatically a deployable tuning rule.
Completed-budget outcomes matter. A method can look slower early because its effective step remains large, then behave differently during decay. An early curve alone is an incomplete comparison.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: The forward function remains a separate question
text:
The forward function remains a separate question
The geometric derivation above works for any matrix proposal. Interpreting its radius as redundant requires a statement about the forward function.
A normalization gain can compensate one matrix’s scale through a joint transformation. That is not the same as independently scaling that matrix with every other parameter fixed. If a gain is shared, compensating it changes every consuming branch. We will examine that compatibility explicitly in Part 11.
Fixed-norm optimization and learned forward scales are therefore not inherently opposed. A method can constrain a directional matrix while another parameter controls a meaningful amplitude. The next post asks which of those amplitudes should remain available.

text:

The trial length is \(0.5\). The angle is \(\arctan(0.5)\) and the chord is approximately \(0.459506\).
Zero. The trial point is \(E/2\), which renormalizes back to \(E\).
\(\alpha=aR_t\eta=0.54\). This matches one direction under the stated common-proposal assumption.
